questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Pine seedlings failing in new soil until mycorrhizal fungi are supplied, contrasted with commensalism
questions.question: Pine seedlings planted in a newly cleared region with no pine trees grew poorly and showed signs of phosphorus deficiency, although the soil contained enough phosphate. When a little soil from an old pine forest was mixed in, the seedlings grew well. Which explanation is correct?
options: A) The forest soil supplied mycorrhizal fungi; the fungal hyphae absorb phosphorus and water from the soil for the pine, and the pine supplies the fungus with carbohydrates, so both partners benefit (mutualism)
B) The forest soil supplied a parasitic fungus that weakened competing weeds
C) The forest soil supplied a commensal fungus that gains food from the pine roots while the pine is neither helped nor harmed
D) The forest soil simply added extra phosphate fertiliser
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Mycorrhizal fungi from the forest soil formed a mutualistic association with the pine roots.
Concept: Mycorrhiza is a close association between a fungus and the roots of a higher plant. The fungal hyphae greatly increase the absorbing surface and take up phosphorus and water for the plant; the plant passes sugars to the fungus. Both partners gain, so it is mutualism (+/+). In commensalism (+/0), one species gains and the other is unaffected, as with an orchid growing on a mango branch or barnacles on a whale.
Why: The soil already had phosphate, so the problem was uptake, not supply. Old pine-forest soil contains the fungal partner; once roots were colonised, phosphorus uptake and growth improved. Many pines cannot grow well at all without mycorrhizae.
Why not the others: (B) Weeds were not the cause of phosphorus deficiency in soil already rich in phosphate, and a parasite harms its host. (C) The pine clearly benefits, so the relationship is not commensal. (D) The soil already had enough phosphate, and a small amount of forest soil adds very little phosphate.
Key point: Mycorrhiza: fungus gives P and water, plant gives sugar, so mutualism (+/+); commensalism is +/0.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Upright and inverted pyramids of number, biomass and energy, and the ten per cent pattern of energy transfer
questions.question: In an ecosystem, producers fix 10,000 J of energy. Which statement about ecological pyramids is correct?
options: A) All three pyramids (number, biomass and energy) are always upright in every ecosystem
B) The pyramid of energy is inverted in the sea because phytoplankton have a small standing crop

C) About 1000 J reaches primary consumers, 100 J secondary consumers and 10 J tertiary consumers, so the pyramid of energy is always upright; the pyramid of numbers can be inverted (one tree supporting many insects), and the pyramid of biomass can be inverted in the sea
D) The pyramid of numbers for a tree ecosystem is always upright, because producers are always the most numerous
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Energy: 10,000 → 1000 → 100 → 10 J, always upright; numbers and biomass can be inverted.
Concept: About 10 per cent of the energy at one trophic level passes to the next (the rest is lost mainly as heat in respiration). The pyramid of energy therefore always narrows upwards. Numbers and biomass are standing measures at one moment, so they can be inverted in special cases.
Why: One large tree (producer) feeds thousands of insects, so the number pyramid is inverted at its base. In the sea, the small standing biomass of fast-reproducing phytoplankton supports a larger biomass of zooplankton and fish, so the biomass pyramid is inverted. Energy flow is measured per unit time and cannot increase up the chain.
Why not the others: (A) Number and biomass pyramids can be inverted. (B) The biomass pyramid, not the energy pyramid, is inverted in the sea. (D) A single tree supports many herbivores, so the pyramid of numbers is inverted there.
Key point: Energy pyramid is always upright (about 10 % transfer); number and biomass pyramids can be inverted.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: How cryopreservation and seed banks conserve species away from their habitat, and what Red Data Books and Ramsar sites are
questions.question: Which statement about conservation is correct?
options: A) Ramsar sites are botanical gardens where rare plants are grown away from their natural habitat

B) In ex situ conservation, gametes, embryos and seeds can be stored for long periods by cryopreservation in liquid nitrogen at about −196 °C, where metabolism almost stops; the IUCN Red Data Book lists threatened species by category; Ramsar sites are wetlands of international importance protected in their natural setting
C) The Red Data Book lists only extinct species
D) Cryopreservation works because very low temperature speeds up cell division
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Cryopreservation at −196 °C halts metabolism; the Red Data Book lists threatened species; Ramsar sites are protected wetlands.
Concept: Ex situ conservation protects species outside their natural habitat: zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks and cryopreservation of gametes and embryos. In situ conservation protects them in their habitat, such as national parks, biosphere reserves and wetlands. The IUCN Red Data Book records the conservation status (critically endangered, endangered, vulnerable and so on) of species.
Why: At −196 °C, biochemical reactions and ice-crystal growth are practically stopped (cells are protected by cryoprotectants), so living material can be stored for many years and revived. Ramsar sites, named after the convention signed at Ramsar, Iran, protect wetlands where they are.
Why not the others: (A) Ramsar sites are wetlands conserved in place, not gardens. (C) The Red Data Book covers threatened categories, not only extinct species. (D) Very low temperature stops metabolism and division; it does not speed them up.
Key point: Ex situ: seed banks, cryopreservation (−196 °C); Red Data Book: threat status; Ramsar: wetlands in situ.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Applying the biological species concept to the results of crosses between populations
questions.question:
The table shows the results of crosses between pairs of animal populations.
| Cross | Offspring | Fertility of offspring |
|---|---|---|
| P: horse × donkey | mule | sterile |
| Q: population of Indian cattle × population of European cattle | calves | fertile |
| R: lion × tiger (in captivity) | liger | males sterile |
| S: two geographically separate populations of house sparrows | chicks | fertile |
On the basis of the biological species concept (interbreeding with fertile offspring), which pairs belong to the same species?
options: A) P and R only
B) P, Q, R and S
C) Q only
D) Q and S only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Q and S only.
Concept: A biological species is a group of natural populations that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring and is reproductively isolated from other such groups. Taxonomy groups organisms by such shared features, and systematics also studies their evolutionary relationships.
Why: Q and S give fertile offspring, so each pair belongs to one species, even though the populations look different or live far apart. P (mule) and R (liger, with sterile males) give hybrids that are sterile or partly sterile, so horse and donkey, and lion and tiger, are separate species (even though lion and tiger share the genus Panthera).
Why not the others: (A) Picks the crosses with sterile hybrids, which shows that those parents belong to different species. (B) Producing offspring is not enough; the offspring must be fertile. (C) Leaves out S; being far apart does not make populations separate species if they can interbreed and produce fertile young.
Key point: Same species means interbreeding with fertile offspring; sterile hybrids mean different species.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Identifying a moss and a fern from which generation is dominant and whether vascular tissue is present
questions.question:
The table describes two plants X and Y.
| Feature | X | Y |
|---|---|---|
| Main plant body | haploid, leafy, attached by rhizoids | diploid, with true roots, stem and leaves |
| Vascular tissue | absent | xylem and phloem present |
| Other generation | diploid capsule on a stalk, attached to and dependent on the main plant | small, free-living, heart-shaped haploid thallus |
Which identification is correct?
options: A) X is a moss such as Funaria (dominant gametophyte, dependent sporophyte); Y is a fern such as Dryopteris (dominant sporophyte, independent prothallus)
B) X is a fern and Y is a moss
C) X is a liverwort with a dominant sporophyte; Y is a gymnosperm with seeds
D) Both X and Y have a dominant sporophyte
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) X is a moss (dominant gametophyte); Y is a fern (dominant sporophyte).
Concept: In bryophytes the main plant is the haploid gametophyte; the diploid sporophyte (foot, seta, capsule) stays attached to it and depends on it for nutrition. In pteridophytes the main plant is the diploid sporophyte, with true roots, stem, leaves and vascular tissue; the gametophyte is a small, free-living prothallus.
Why: X has a haploid leafy body with rhizoids, no vascular tissue and a dependent capsule: a moss. Y has a diploid vascular body and a heart-shaped prothallus: a fern.
Why not the others: (B) Reverses the two groups. (C) A liverwort also has a dominant gametophyte, and Y has no seeds; the free-living prothallus marks a pteridophyte. (D) X's dominant body is haploid, so it is the gametophyte.
Key point: Bryophytes: dominant gametophyte, no vascular tissue; pteridophytes: dominant vascular sporophyte, free prothallus.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Placing a plant in Fabaceae from its floral features and predicting where its seeds are borne
questions.question: A plant has flowers with the following features: the flower can be cut into two equal halves along one plane only; the largest petal (standard) overlaps the two lateral petals, which overlap the two lowest petals; there are ten stamens, nine fused by their filaments and one free; the ovary has one carpel. What else would you expect?
options: A) Actinomorphic flowers with valvate aestivation and axile placentation
B) A family with fused anthers and a bicarpellary ovary with free-central placentation
C) Zygomorphic flowers with vexillary aestivation, diadelphous stamens, and marginal placentation, so the seeds are borne along one side of a pod (as in pea, family Fabaceae)
D) An ovary with many carpels, each with a single basal ovule
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Zygomorphic, vexillary, diadelphous, marginal placentation: Fabaceae (pea family).
Concept: Symmetry: actinomorphic flowers can be divided into equal halves along any radial plane; zygomorphic along only one. Aestivation is the arrangement of petals in the bud; vexillary (papilionaceous) aestivation has a large standard, two wings and a keel. Placentation is the arrangement of ovules in the ovary; in marginal placentation, ovules are in rows along the ventral suture of a single carpel.
Why: One plane of symmetry means zygomorphic; standard overlapping wings overlapping keel is vexillary; (9) + 1 stamens are diadelphous; a single carpel with marginal placentation forms a pod (legume) with seeds along one margin. These are the features of Fabaceae.
Why not the others: (A) Contradicts the single plane of symmetry and the overlapping petals. (B) Fused anthers (syngenesious) and free-central placentation are not features of this flower, which has one carpel. (D) The flower has only one carpel.
Key point: Fabaceae: zygomorphic, vexillary, (9)+1 diadelphous stamens, monocarpellary with marginal placentation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Using the number of xylem and phloem strands in a transverse section to tell a monocot root from a dicot root
questions.question: A transverse section of a young root shows a total of 18 separate strands of xylem and phloem, arranged on alternate radii, with a large, well-developed pith. A second root shows 8 such strands in total, with little or no pith. How many xylem bundles does each root have, and which is the monocot root?
options: A) 18 and 8; the second root is monocot
B) 9 and 4; the first root is monocot (polyarch) and the second is dicot (tetrarch)
C) 9 and 4; the first root is dicot and the second is monocot
D) 6 and 2; both are dicot roots
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 9 and 4; the first root is monocot (polyarch), the second dicot (tetrarch).
Concept: In roots the vascular bundles are radial: xylem and phloem strands lie on alternate radii, in equal numbers. Dicot roots usually have 2 to 4 xylem bundles (diarch to tetrarch) and little or no pith; monocot roots usually have more than six (polyarch) and a large pith.
Given: root 1: 18 strands in total, large pith; root 2: 8 strands in total, little pith.
Formula/Principle: xylem strands = phloem strands = half the total in a radial arrangement.
Step 1: Root 1: 18 ÷ 2 = 9 xylem bundles: polyarch, monocot.
Step 2: Root 2: 8 ÷ 2 = 4 xylem bundles: tetrarch, dicot.
Why: The count of xylem bundles and the size of the pith together distinguish the two roots; secondary growth (seen later in dicot roots) is absent in monocot roots.
Why not the others: (A) Counts all strands as xylem; half are phloem. (C) Reverses the two roots; many xylem bundles and a large pith mean monocot. (D) Divides by three; the strands alternate one to one.
Key point: Radial bundles: xylem = phloem; polyarch with large pith means monocot root, 2–4 bundles means dicot root.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Path of blood through the frog heart, and the portal systems of the frog
questions.question: Which sequence correctly traces deoxygenated blood returning from the body of a frog until it leaves the heart?
options: A) Venae cavae → left atrium → ventricle → pulmonary veins
B) Venae cavae → right atrium → right ventricle → left ventricle → aorta
C) Pulmonary veins → right atrium → sinus venosus → ventricle
D) Venae cavae → sinus venosus → right atrium → ventricle → conus (truncus) arteriosus → arterial arches
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Venae cavae → sinus venosus → right atrium → ventricle → conus arteriosus → arterial arches.
Concept: The frog heart has three chambers: two atria and one ventricle. A triangular sinus venosus collects blood from the venae cavae and opens into the right atrium; the ventricle opens into a conus (truncus) arteriosus. Oxygenated blood from the lungs returns by the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. Frogs also have a hepatic portal system (gut to liver) and a renal portal system (hind limbs to kidneys).
Why: Both atria empty into the single ventricle, from which blood passes into the conus arteriosus and then to the arterial arches that supply the body, head and lungs and skin.
Why not the others: (A) Body blood enters the right side through the sinus venosus, and pulmonary veins carry blood to the heart, not away from it. (B) The frog has only one ventricle. (C) Pulmonary veins drain into the left atrium, not into the right atrium or sinus venosus.
Key point: Frog: sinus venosus → right atrium → single ventricle → conus arteriosus; pulmonary veins → left atrium.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Why antibiotics that act on 70S ribosomes kill bacteria without stopping protein synthesis in human cells
questions.question: Antibiotics such as streptomycin and erythromycin block protein synthesis in bacteria but have little effect on protein synthesis in the cytoplasm of human cells. Which explanation is correct?
options: A) Human cells do not make proteins on ribosomes

B) These antibiotics bind to the 70S ribosomes (30S and 50S subunits) of prokaryotes, which differ from the 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes (40S and 60S) of eukaryotes; human mitochondria, which have 70S-type ribosomes, can be partly affected
C) Bacterial ribosomes are enclosed in a nuclear membrane that the antibiotics dissolve
D) Prokaryotic cells have a nucleus, so the antibiotics act on their DNA
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The antibiotics act on prokaryotic 70S ribosomes, which differ from eukaryotic 80S ribosomes.
Concept: Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles, and have 70S ribosomes (50S + 30S). Eukaryotic cells have 80S ribosomes (60S + 40S) in the cytoplasm, while mitochondria and chloroplasts contain 70S ribosomes, which supports the idea that these organelles arose from bacteria.
Why: Because the ribosomes differ in structure, a drug can bind the bacterial ribosome and stop translation without blocking the host's cytoplasmic ribosomes. This selective target makes such drugs useful antibiotics.
Why not the others: (A) All cells make proteins on ribosomes. (C) Prokaryotes have no nuclear membrane, and ribosomes are not enclosed in membranes. (D) Prokaryotes have no true nucleus, and these drugs act on ribosomes, not DNA.
Key point: Prokaryotes: 70S ribosomes; eukaryotic cytoplasm: 80S; selective drug target.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Number of chromosomes, chromatids and amount of DNA at stages of mitosis and meiosis for a cell with 2n = 16
questions.question: A diploid cell has 2n = 16 chromosomes and a DNA content of 2C in G1. What is (i) the number of chromosomes in the cell at anaphase of mitosis, (ii) the DNA content of the whole cell at anaphase I of meiosis, and (iii) the number of chromatids in each cell at metaphase II?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 32; 4C; 16.
Concept: DNA doubles in S phase (2C → 4C) while the chromosome number stays 2n, each chromosome now having two sister chromatids. In mitotic anaphase the centromeres split, so each chromatid counts as a chromosome. In anaphase I homologous chromosomes separate but sister chromatids stay joined. After meiosis I each cell is haploid (n), with each chromosome still having two chromatids.
Given: 2n = 16; DNA = 2C in G1, so 4C after S phase.
Formula/Principle: chromosomes are counted by centromeres; chromatids = 2 per chromosome until the centromeres split.
Step 1: (i) Mitotic anaphase: 16 × 2 = 32 chromosomes in the cell before it divides.
Step 2: (ii) Anaphase I: the cell has not divided yet, so DNA is still 4C.
Step 3: (iii) Metaphase II: n = 8 chromosomes, each with 2 chromatids = 16 chromatids (DNA 2C).
Why: Chromatid separation doubles the chromosome count only in mitotic anaphase and anaphase II; meiosis I halves the chromosome number without splitting centromeres.
Why not the others: (A) Ignores DNA replication and the split of centromeres. (B) The DNA content does not halve until the cell divides at the end of meiosis I, and a metaphase II cell is haploid. (C) Ignores the split of centromeres in mitotic anaphase and miscounts the chromatids.
Key point: Mitotic anaphase: 4n chromosomes; anaphase I: 4C; metaphase II: n chromosomes, 2n chromatids.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Effect of illuminating chloroplasts with only far-red light beyond 680 nm on the products of the light reaction
questions.question: Isolated chloroplasts are illuminated only with far-red light of wavelength longer than 690 nm, which is absorbed by photosystem I but hardly at all by photosystem II. Which result is expected?
options: A) ATP is still formed by cyclic photophosphorylation around PSI, but NADPH is not formed and no oxygen is released
B) Both ATP and NADPH are formed, and oxygen is released
C) No ATP is formed, but oxygen is released
D) NADPH is formed and oxygen is released, but no ATP is formed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Cyclic photophosphorylation gives ATP only; no NADPH and no O₂.
Concept: In non-cyclic electron flow, PSII (P680) splits water (releasing O₂) and passes electrons through the electron transport chain to PSI (P700) and then to NADP⁺, making NADPH, with ATP formed by chemiosmosis. When only PSI is excited, electrons from P700 return through the cytochrome complex to PSI (cyclic flow), pumping protons and making ATP only.
Why: Without PSII activity, water is not split, so there is no O₂ and no supply of electrons to make NADPH. The fall in photosynthesis in light beyond 680 nm (the red drop) shows that both photosystems are needed for full activity.
Why not the others: (B) Needs PSII, which far-red light does not drive. (C) Oxygen release needs PSII, while ATP can still be made. (D) NADPH and O₂ both need non-cyclic flow starting at PSII.
Key point: PSI alone: cyclic flow, ATP only; PSII is needed for O₂ and NADPH.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Finding the respiratory substrate of germinating seeds from respirometer readings, and how fats enter respiration
questions.question: Two identical respirometers contain equal masses of germinating seeds. In set 1, a tube of KOH absorbs carbon dioxide; in set 2, there is no KOH. In the same time, the gas volume falls by 10.0 mL in set 1 and by 3.0 mL in set 2. What is the respiratory quotient, which substrate is being respired, and how does it enter the respiratory pathway?
options: A) 0.30; protein; as amino acids entering glycolysis directly
B) 1.0; carbohydrate; as glucose
C) 0.70; fat; fatty acids are broken down to acetyl CoA, which enters the Krebs cycle, and glycerol enters glycolysis as PGAL
D) 1.43; organic acids; through the Krebs cycle
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) RQ = 0.70: fat, entering as acetyl CoA (fatty acids) and PGAL (glycerol).
Concept: RQ = volume of CO₂ released ÷ volume of O₂ consumed. KOH removes CO₂, so the fall in set 1 equals the O₂ used; in set 2 the fall is O₂ used minus CO₂ released. RQ is 1 for carbohydrate, about 0.7 for fat (for example tripalmitin: 2C₅₁H₉₈O₆ + 145O₂ → 102CO₂ + 98H₂O, RQ = 102/145 ≈ 0.7) and about 0.9 for protein. Respiration is amphibolic: its intermediates are used both to break down and to build molecules.
Given: fall in set 1 = 10.0 mL (O₂ used); fall in set 2 = 3.0 mL.
Formula/Principle: CO₂ released = O₂ used − fall in set 2; RQ = CO₂/O₂.
Step 1: CO₂ released = 10.0 − 3.0 = 7.0 mL.
Step 2: RQ = 7.0 ÷ 10.0 = 0.70: fat (as in oil-rich seeds such as groundnut or castor).
Why: Fats are poor in oxygen, so more O₂ is needed to oxidise them than CO₂ is released. Fatty acids enter as acetyl CoA, and glycerol is converted to PGAL, an intermediate of glycolysis.
Why not the others: (A) Takes the set 2 reading as the CO₂ released; it is the difference between O₂ used and CO₂ released. (B) RQ = 1 would give no volume change in set 2. (D) Inverts the ratio (O₂/CO₂).
Key point: KOH set gives O₂ used; CO₂ = O₂ − (fall without KOH); RQ 0.7 means fat.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting iodine tests on tubes of starch with saliva under different conditions to find what salivary amylase needs
questions.question:
Four tubes each contain 5 mL of starch solution, and are kept for 20 minutes as shown, then tested with iodine solution.
| Tube | Added | Conditions | Colour with iodine |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 mL fresh saliva | 37 °C, pH 6.8 | yellow-brown |
| 2 | 1 mL boiled and cooled saliva | 37 °C, pH 6.8 | blue-black |
| 3 | 1 mL fresh saliva | 37 °C, pH 2 | blue-black |
| 4 | 1 mL fresh saliva | 0 °C (ice), pH 6.8 | blue-black |
Which conclusion is correct?
options: A) Saliva digests starch only in an acidic medium
B) Boiling increases the activity of salivary amylase
C) Salivary amylase is inactive at 37 °C
D) Salivary amylase digests starch (tube 1, no starch left) only when active; it is destroyed by boiling (tube 2), inactive at very low pH (tube 3, as in the stomach) and very slow at 0 °C (tube 4)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Amylase works at body temperature and near-neutral pH; boiling denatures it; low pH and cold stop or slow it.
Concept: Salivary amylase (ptyalin) breaks starch down to maltose; its best conditions are about pH 6.8 and 37 °C. Iodine gives a blue-black colour with starch and stays yellow-brown when starch is absent.
Why: Only tube 1 lost its starch. Tube 2 is the control that proves the effect is due to an enzyme (a protein denatured by heat). Tube 3 shows why starch digestion by saliva stops in the acidic stomach. At 0 °C molecules move slowly, so activity is very low; this inactivation by cold is reversible on warming.
Why not the others: (A) Tube 3 (pH 2) still contains starch. (B) Boiled saliva left the starch undigested. (C) Tube 1, at 37 °C, digested the starch completely.
Key point: Salivary amylase: active at 37 °C and about pH 6.8; denatured by boiling; stopped by acid.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Changes in sarcomere bands during contraction, and the roles of actin, myosin, troponin and calcium
questions.question: Which statement correctly compares the thick and thin filaments and the changes in a sarcomere when a skeletal muscle contracts?
options: A) Thick filaments are myosin and thin filaments are actin with tropomyosin and troponin; during contraction the A band keeps its length while the I band and H zone shorten and the Z lines move closer, because Ca²⁺ binds troponin, exposing sites on actin for myosin heads to pull the thin filaments inward
B) During contraction the actin and myosin filaments themselves shorten, so all bands shorten equally
C) The A band shortens while the I band stays the same length
D) Ca²⁺ binds to myosin and covers the binding sites on actin, causing relaxation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A band constant; I band and H zone shorten; Ca²⁺ binds troponin, exposing myosin-binding sites on actin.
Concept: A sarcomere runs from one Z line to the next. The A band is the length of the thick (myosin) filaments; the I band contains only thin (actin) filaments; the H zone is the middle of the A band with no overlap. Sliding filament theory: thin filaments slide over thick filaments without either changing length.
Why: When Ca²⁺ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, it binds troponin, which moves tropomyosin off the active sites on actin. Myosin heads, energised by ATP hydrolysis, form cross bridges and pull actin towards the M line. Overlap increases, so the I band and H zone narrow while the A band stays the same.
Why not the others: (B) The filaments slide past each other; they do not shorten. (C) The A band is set by the length of myosin filaments, which does not change. (D) Ca²⁺ binds troponin, not myosin, and its binding starts contraction, not relaxation.
Key point: Contraction: A band constant; I band and H zone shorten; Ca²⁺–troponin unmasks actin.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Effects of a drug that blocks parasympathetic action on organs supplied by both divisions of the autonomic nervous system
questions.question: A drug blocks the action of acetylcholine at the junctions between parasympathetic nerve fibres and the organs they supply, without affecting the sympathetic division. Which set of effects is expected?
options: A) Slower heart rate, constricted pupils, more saliva and faster movement of the gut
B) Faster heart rate, dilated pupils, reduced salivation and slower movement of the gut, because the sympathetic effects are no longer opposed
C) No effect, because the autonomic nervous system works only during sleep
D) Paralysis of skeletal muscles of the limbs
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Faster heart, dilated pupils, dry mouth, slower gut.
Concept: The peripheral nervous system has a somatic part (to skeletal muscles) and an autonomic (visceral) part, which controls involuntary organs. The autonomic part has sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions that usually act on the same organ in opposite ways. Parasympathetic nerves slow the heart, constrict the pupils, increase salivation and stimulate digestion ("rest and digest"); sympathetic nerves do the opposite ("fight or flight").
Why: When parasympathetic action is blocked, the sympathetic division acts unopposed, so the organ responses shift to the sympathetic pattern. Drugs of this kind (such as atropine) are used to dilate the pupils during eye examination.
Why not the others: (A) These are parasympathetic effects, which the drug blocks. (C) The autonomic nervous system works all the time, controlling heart rate and digestion. (D) Skeletal muscles are controlled by the somatic nervous system, which the drug does not affect.
Key point: Sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions oppose each other; block one and the other's effects dominate.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting a foetal karyotype obtained by amniocentesis, and the legal misuse of the test
questions.question: In a pregnancy at about 16 weeks, a sample of amniotic fluid is taken and cells in it are cultured and examined. Their karyotype shows 47 chromosomes, with three copies of chromosome 21 and two X chromosomes. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) The cells are from the mother, so the mother has Down syndrome
B) The foetus is male with Klinefelter syndrome

C) The cells are foetal cells shed into the amniotic fluid, so the foetus is female with trisomy 21 (Down syndrome); amniocentesis is used to detect such chromosomal disorders, and its use only to find the sex of the foetus is banned in India
D) The result shows that the foetus has a sexually transmitted infection
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The foetus is female with trisomy 21 (Down syndrome); using amniocentesis to determine sex alone is illegal.
Concept: Amniocentesis is a prenatal test in which a little amniotic fluid is withdrawn. The fluid contains cells shed by the foetus, which can be cultured and karyotyped to detect chromosomal abnormalities such as trisomy 21. Because it was misused for sex determination leading to female foeticide, its use for this purpose is legally banned in India.
Why: 47 chromosomes with three copies of chromosome 21 means trisomy 21; XX means a female foetus. Sexually transmitted infections (such as gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes and HIV) are diagnosed by other tests, not by a karyotype.
Why not the others: (A) Amniotic fluid cells come from the foetus, not the mother. (B) Klinefelter syndrome is XXY with 47 chromosomes; here the extra chromosome is 21 and the sex chromosomes are XX. (D) A karyotype shows chromosomes, not infections.
Key point: Amniocentesis: karyotype of foetal cells detects trisomies; banned for sex determination.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing a dihybrid test cross that gives 1:1:1:1 with one that shows linkage, and finding the recombination frequency
questions.question: Two test crosses are made, each between a plant heterozygous for two genes and a double-recessive plant. Cross 1 (genes A and B) gives 252 : 248 : 250 : 250 for the four phenotypes. Cross 2 (genes C and D, the dihybrid formed from CCDD × ccdd) gives CD 410, cd 410, Cd 90, cD 90. Which conclusion is correct?
options: A) Genes A and B assort independently; genes C and D are linked with a recombination frequency of 18 %
B) Both pairs of genes assort independently
C) Genes C and D are linked with a recombination frequency of 82 %
D) Genes A and B are linked, and C and D assort independently
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A and B assort independently; C and D are linked with 18 % recombination.
Concept: A dihybrid test cross gives four phenotypes in a 1:1:1:1 ratio if the genes are on different chromosomes (independent assortment, giving 9:3:3:1 in an F₂). If the genes are linked, the parental types are much more common than the recombinant types, and the recombination frequency = recombinants ÷ total × 100.
Given: Cross 1: about 250 of each; Cross 2: parental CD 410, cd 410, recombinant Cd 90, cD 90.
Formula/Principle: recombination frequency = (recombinants ÷ total) × 100.
Step 1: Cross 2 total = 410 + 410 + 90 + 90 = 1000; recombinants = 180.
Step 2: Recombination frequency = 180 ÷ 1000 × 100 = 18 %.
Why: The parental types (CD, cd) match the original parents, so they result from no crossing over; Cd and cD arise by crossing over between the linked genes. The lower the frequency, the closer the genes are on the chromosome.
Why not the others: (B) Cross 2 departs strongly from 1:1:1:1. (C) 82 % is the frequency of parental types; recombination frequency cannot exceed 50 %. (D) Reverses the two crosses.
Key point: Test cross 1:1:1:1 means independent; excess parentals mean linkage; RF = recombinants ÷ total.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing what Griffith, Avery–MacLeod–McCarty and Hershey–Chase each showed about the genetic material
questions.question: Which statement correctly matches each experiment with what it established?
options: A) Griffith proved that DNA is the genetic material by treating extracts with DNase
B) Hershey and Chase found that heat-killed S bacteria kill mice by themselves
C) Avery, MacLeod and McCarty showed that proteins carry the transforming principle, because protease stopped transformation

D) Griffith showed that some "transforming principle" from heat-killed S bacteria converted live R bacteria into virulent S bacteria, without identifying it; Avery, MacLeod and McCarty showed it was DNA, since only DNase stopped transformation; Hershey and Chase showed that the DNA of a bacteriophage, not its protein, enters the bacterium
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Griffith: transformation occurs; Avery et al.: the agent is DNA; Hershey–Chase: phage DNA enters the host.
Concept: Griffith (1928) injected mice with Streptococcus pneumoniae: live R (non-virulent) cells or heat-killed S cells alone did not kill, but a mixture of the two did, and live S cells were recovered. Avery, MacLeod and McCarty (1944) purified the components of heat-killed S cells: transformation was stopped by DNase but not by protease or RNase. Hershey and Chase (1952) labelled phage DNA with ³²P and protein with ³⁵S; only ³²P entered the infected bacteria.
Why: Each experiment answered a further question: does genetic transfer happen, what molecule carries it, and does the same hold in viruses.
Why not the others: (A) Griffith did not identify the chemical; DNase was used by Avery and colleagues. (B) Heat-killed S cells alone did not kill mice, and this was Griffith's experiment. (C) Protease did not stop transformation; DNase did.
Key point: Griffith: transformation; Avery et al.: DNA is the transforming principle; Hershey–Chase: phage DNA enters.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Ordering the steps of sewage treatment from primary treatment to biogas production in sludge digesters
questions.question: The steps of a sewage treatment plant are listed in random order. P: the effluent from primary treatment is agitated in large aeration tanks, where aerobic microbes grow as flocs and reduce the BOD. Q: floating debris is removed by filtration and grit is allowed to settle, forming primary sludge. R: the effluent with much lower BOD is released into a river. S: the bulk of the settled activated sludge is pumped into anaerobic digesters, where bacteria produce methane, hydrogen sulphide and carbon dioxide. T: the flocs are allowed to settle in a settling tank, and a small part of this activated sludge is returned to the aeration tank as an inoculum. Which is the correct order?
options: A) P → Q → T → S → R
B) Q → P → T → S, with the treated effluent released (R) after settling
C) Q → T → P → R → S
D) S → Q → P → T → R
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Q → P → T → S, with R after settling.
Concept: Primary treatment removes particles physically (filtration and sedimentation). Secondary (biological) treatment uses aerobic heterotrophic microbes in flocs (bacteria with fungal filaments) to consume organic matter, sharply lowering the BOD. The activated sludge settles; some is recycled as an inoculum, and the rest is digested anaerobically, producing biogas.
Why: Physical removal must come first; biological oxidation needs aeration; settling separates the sludge from the effluent; the anaerobic digestion of sludge gives a mixture of gases that can be used as fuel. The effluent, now low in BOD, can be released after settling (step R).
Why not the others: (A) Aeration cannot come before primary treatment removes the debris. (C) Flocs form in the aeration tank, so they cannot settle before aeration. (D) Digesters handle activated sludge, which forms only after secondary treatment.
Key point: Primary (physical) → aeration with flocs (BOD falls) → settling and recycling → anaerobic digestion gives biogas.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Palindromic recognition site, sticky ends and expected cutting frequency for an enzyme that recognises GGATCC
questions.question: A restriction endonuclease recognises the sequence 5′-GGATCC-3′ and cuts each strand between the two G nucleotides. Which statement is correct?
options: A) The enzyme cuts both strands at the same point, producing only blunt ends that cannot pair with any other fragment
B) The enzyme recognises any six bases, regardless of their order

C) The site is a palindrome (the complementary strand also reads 5′-GGATCC-3′); the staggered cuts leave single-stranded 5′-GATC overhangs (sticky ends) that can pair with ends cut by the same enzyme and then be sealed by DNA ligase; in random DNA such a six-base site is expected about once in 4096 base pairs
D) DNA ligase cuts the DNA at the recognition site
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Palindromic site, sticky 5′-GATC overhangs, sealed by ligase; expected about once every 4⁶ = 4096 bp.
Concept: A restriction endonuclease cuts DNA at a specific recognition sequence, usually a palindrome that reads the same on both strands in the 5′ → 3′ direction. Cutting a little away from the centre leaves short single-stranded overhangs (sticky ends). DNA ligase joins the sugar-phosphate backbones.
Why: The complement of 5′-GGATCC-3′, read 5′ → 3′, is also GGATCC. The G↓GATCC cut on both strands leaves four-base 5′ overhangs. If vector and foreign DNA are cut by the same enzyme, their ends are complementary and can be joined. The chance of a given six-base sequence at a random position is (1/4)⁶ = 1/4096.
Why not the others: (A) This cut is staggered, giving sticky ends rather than blunt ends. (B) Restriction enzymes are highly specific for one sequence. (D) Ligase joins DNA; it does not cut it.
Key point: Restriction site: palindrome, staggered cut, sticky ends; ligase seals; six-base site about once per 4096 bp.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Formal charges on the atoms of ozone and nitrous oxide from their Lewis structures
questions.question:
The table gives the electron count for each atom in one Lewis structure of ozone, O_a=O_b–O_c, and of nitrous oxide, N_a≡N_b–O.
| Atom | Valence electrons | Lone-pair electrons | Bonding electrons |
|---|---|---|---|
| O_a (ozone) | 6 | 4 | 4 |
| O_b (ozone, central) | 6 | 2 | 6 |
| O_c (ozone) | 6 | 6 | 2 |
| N_a (N₂O) | 5 | 2 | 6 |
| N_b (N₂O, central) | 5 | 0 | 8 |
| O (N₂O) | 6 | 6 | 2 |
What are the formal charges on O_b, O_c and N_b?
options: A) 0, 0 and 0
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) +1, −1 and +1.
Concept: Formal charge = valence electrons − lone-pair electrons − ½ (bonding electrons). It is a bookkeeping charge that helps choose the best Lewis structure; the formal charges in a neutral molecule add up to zero.
Given: O_b: 6, 2, 6; O_c: 6, 6, 2; N_b: 5, 0, 8.
Formula/Principle: FC = V − L − B/2.
Step 1: O_b: 6 − 2 − 3 = +1; O_c: 6 − 6 − 1 = −1; O_a: 6 − 4 − 2 = 0. Sum for ozone = 0.
Step 2: N_b: 5 − 0 − 4 = +1; N_a: 5 − 2 − 3 = 0; O: 6 − 6 − 1 = −1. Sum for N₂O = 0.
Why: Both molecules are neutral, so the charges cancel; the central atom carries the positive formal charge in each structure shown. The real ozone molecule is a resonance hybrid, with the negative charge shared between the two end oxygens.
Why not the others: (A) Ignores the unequal sharing of electrons in the Lewis structure. (B) Reverses the sign for O_b and O_c. (C) Gets ozone right but omits the formal charge on the central nitrogen, which has no lone pair and four bonds.
Key point: FC = V − L − B/2; the formal charges add up to the overall charge.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Converting an internal energy change into an enthalpy change for the synthesis of ammonia, and comparing with the combustion of carbon
questions.question: At 298 K, the internal energy change for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) is ΔU = −87.1 kJ. What is ΔH for this reaction, and how do ΔH and ΔU compare for C(graphite) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g) at the same temperature? (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
options: A) −82.1 kJ; ΔH is more negative than ΔU for the carbon reaction
B) −92.1 kJ; ΔH = ΔU for the carbon reaction
C) −87.1 kJ; ΔH = ΔU for both reactions
D) −92.1 kJ; ΔH is less negative than ΔU for the carbon reaction
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ΔH = −92.1 kJ; for carbon combustion ΔH = ΔU.
Concept: ΔH = ΔU + Δ(PV). For ideal gases at constant temperature, Δ(PV) = Δn_g RT, where Δn_g is moles of gaseous products minus moles of gaseous reactants. Solids and liquids contribute almost nothing.
Given: ΔU = −87.1 kJ; T = 298 K; R = 8.314 × 10⁻³ kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
Formula/Principle: ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT.
Step 1: Ammonia synthesis: Δn_g = 2 − (1 + 3) = −2.
Step 2: ΔH = −87.1 + (−2)(8.314 × 10⁻³)(298) = −87.1 − 4.96 ≈ −92.1 kJ.
Step 3: Carbon combustion: Δn_g = 1 − 1 = 0 (graphite is a solid), so ΔH = ΔU.
Why: When the number of gas moles decreases, the surroundings do work on the system at constant pressure, so ΔH is more negative than ΔU. With no change in gas moles there is no PV work.
Why not the others: (A) Uses the wrong sign for Δn_g, and Δn_g = 0 for carbon. (C) Ignores the change in moles of gas in ammonia synthesis. (D) The value is right for ammonia, but ΔH equals ΔU for the carbon reaction.
Key point: ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT; count only gas moles.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Effect of adding an inert gas at constant volume and at constant pressure, adding product and heating, on the dissociation of PCl₅
questions.question: The equilibrium PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g), ΔH > 0, is set up in a closed vessel. Which statement about disturbing it is correct?
options: A) Adding argon at constant volume does not shift the equilibrium; adding argon at constant total pressure shifts it forward (more PCl₅ dissociates); adding Cl₂ shifts it backward; raising the temperature shifts it forward and increases K
B) Adding argon at constant volume shifts the equilibrium forward, because the total pressure increases
C) Raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium backward, because heat is a product
D) Adding a catalyst increases the yield of PCl₃ at equilibrium
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Argon at constant V: no shift; argon at constant P: forward; extra Cl₂: backward; heating: forward, K rises.
Concept: Le Chatelier's principle: a system at equilibrium responds to a change so as to partly undo it. Only changes in partial pressures (concentrations) or temperature shift the position; only temperature changes K.
Why: At constant volume, argon raises the total pressure but leaves the partial pressures of the reacting gases unchanged, so Q stays equal to K. At constant total pressure, argon makes the volume larger, lowering all partial pressures; the side with more gas moles (the right side, 2 mol against 1) is favoured. Adding Cl₂ makes Q > K, so the reaction goes backward. The forward reaction is endothermic, so heating favours it and increases K.
Why not the others: (B) The partial pressures of the reacting gases do not change at constant volume, so there is no shift. (C) ΔH > 0 means heat is absorbed by the forward reaction (heat is effectively a reactant), so heating shifts it forward. (D) A catalyst speeds up both directions equally and does not change the equilibrium composition.
Key point: Inert gas: constant V gives no shift, constant P favours more gas moles; only temperature changes K.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Kp from the degree of dissociation of N₂O₄, and the total pressure that halves the degree of dissociation
questions.question: For N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) at a fixed temperature, the degree of dissociation of N₂O₄ is 0.20 when the total equilibrium pressure is 1.00 atm. What is Kp, and at what total pressure (same temperature) would the degree of dissociation be 0.10?
options: B) 0.167 atm; 2.0 atm
C) 0.167 atm; about 4.1 atm
D) 0.20 atm; about 4.1 atm
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Kp ≈ 0.167 atm; about 4.1 atm.
Concept: For a dissociation with degree α starting from 1 mol of N₂O₄, the equilibrium amounts are (1 − α) mol N₂O₄ and 2α mol NO₂, a total of (1 + α) mol. Partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure.
Given: α = 0.20 at P = 1.00 atm.
Formula/Principle: Kp = p(NO₂)²/p(N₂O₄) = [2α/(1 + α)]²P ÷ [(1 − α)/(1 + α)]P = 4α²P/(1 − α²).
Step 1: Kp = 4(0.04)(1.00)/(1 − 0.04) = 0.16/0.96 ≈ 0.167 atm.
Step 2: For α = 0.10: 4(0.01)P/0.99 = 0.167, so P = 0.167 × 0.99/0.04 ≈ 4.1 atm.
Why: Raising the pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles (N₂O₄), so a higher pressure is needed to cut α in half. For small α, α ≈ √(Kp/4P), so halving α needs roughly four times the pressure.
Why not the others: (A) Uses Kp = α²P (forgets the 2 in 2α and the total moles) and lowers the pressure, which would increase α. (B) Kp is right, but doubling the pressure does not halve α; α varies roughly as 1/√P. (D) Takes Kp = α, which has no basis in the equilibrium expression.
Key point: N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂: Kp = 4α²P/(1 − α²); for small α, α ∝ 1/√P.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Balancing the oxidation of iodide by permanganate in neutral and in acidic solution by the ion-electron method
questions.question: Permanganate oxidises iodide in two ways. In neutral or faintly alkaline solution, MnO₄⁻ is reduced to MnO₂ and I⁻ is oxidised to IO₃⁻. In acidic solution, MnO₄⁻ is reduced to Mn²⁺ and I⁻ is oxidised to I₂. How many moles of MnO₄⁻ react with one mole of I⁻ in each case?
options: A) 2 in neutral solution and 0.2 in acidic solution
B) 1 in neutral solution and 1 in acidic solution
C) 0.5 in neutral solution and 5 in acidic solution
D) 6 in neutral solution and 2 in acidic solution
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2 mol (neutral) and 0.2 mol (acidic).
Concept: In a balanced redox equation, the electrons lost by the reducing agent equal the electrons gained by the oxidising agent. The change in oxidation number gives the electrons per particle.
Given: neutral: Mn +7 → +4, I −1 → +5; acidic: Mn +7 → +2, I −1 → 0.
Formula/Principle: moles of MnO₄⁻ × electrons gained each = moles of I⁻ × electrons lost each.
Step 1: Neutral: MnO₄⁻ gains 3 e⁻, I⁻ loses 6 e⁻, so 2MnO₄⁻ react with 1I⁻: 2MnO₄⁻ + I⁻ + H₂O → 2MnO₂ + IO₃⁻ + 2OH⁻.
Step 2: Acidic: MnO₄⁻ gains 5 e⁻, I⁻ loses 1 e⁻, so 2MnO₄⁻ react with 10I⁻: 2MnO₄⁻ + 10I⁻ + 16H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 5I₂ + 8H₂O; ratio 2 : 10 = 0.2.
Why: Checking the neutral equation: O, 9 on each side; H, 2 on each side; charge, −3 on each side. In acid, charge: −2 − 10 + 16 = +4 on the left and +4 on the right.
Why not the others: (B) Ignores the different numbers of electrons transferred. (C) Inverts both ratios (moles of I⁻ per mole of MnO₄⁻). (D) Uses the electron counts themselves rather than balancing them.
Key point: Balance electrons: neutral 2MnO₄⁻ : 1I⁻ (to IO₃⁻); acidic 2MnO₄⁻ : 10I⁻ (to I₂).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.sub_topic: Why the sodium fusion extract is boiled with nitric acid before testing for halogens, and why hydrazine gives no nitrogen test
questions.question: Which statement about Lassaigne's (sodium fusion) test is correct?
options: A) The extract is boiled with dilute HNO₃ so that it can dissolve silver halides
B) Hydrazine (N₂H₄) gives a strong Prussian blue colour, because it is rich in nitrogen
C) Nitric acid is added to convert halide ions into free halogens

D) Before adding AgNO₃ to test for halogens, the extract is boiled with dilute HNO₃ to decompose any NaCN and Na₂S, which would otherwise give precipitates of AgCN or Ag₂S; hydrazine gives no nitrogen test because it contains no carbon, so NaCN cannot form on fusion
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) HNO₃ removes cyanide and sulphide before the halide test; hydrazine has no carbon, so no NaCN forms.
Concept: Fusing an organic compound with sodium converts covalent N, S and halogens into ionic NaCN, Na₂S and NaX. Nitrogen is detected as Prussian blue (from NaCN and iron salts); halogens as silver halide precipitates with AgNO₃ in nitric acid.
Why: Cyanide and sulphide ions also precipitate silver ions, which would give a false positive for halogens. Boiling with HNO₃ drives them off as HCN and H₂S. Nitrogen is detected only as cyanide, which needs both carbon and nitrogen; in hydrazine there is no carbon, so the test fails even though nitrogen is present.
Why not the others: (A) Nitric acid is added to remove interfering ions, not to dissolve the silver halides it is meant to reveal. (B) Hydrazine has no carbon, so it gives no Prussian blue. (C) Nitric acid does not convert halide ions to halogens in this test; the halide ions are precipitated by Ag⁺.
Key point: Boil with HNO₃ to remove CN⁻ and S²⁻ before the AgNO₃ test; N is detected only if C is present (as CN⁻).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Preparing cis- and trans-but-2-ene from but-2-yne, and comparing their boiling and melting points
questions.question: But-2-yne is reduced in two experiments. In experiment 1 it is treated with H₂ over palladium on charcoal partly poisoned with quinoline (Lindlar's catalyst); in experiment 2 it is treated with sodium in liquid ammonia. Which observation is correct about the products?
options: A) Both experiments give the same isomer, which is butane
B) Experiment 1 gives trans-but-2-ene and experiment 2 gives cis-but-2-ene
C) Experiment 1 gives cis-but-2-ene, which has the higher boiling point (it is polar); experiment 2 gives trans-but-2-ene, which has the higher melting point (it packs better in the crystal)
D) The two isomers have the same boiling and melting points
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Lindlar gives cis (higher boiling point); Na/NH₃ gives trans (higher melting point).
Concept: Geometrical isomers arise when rotation about a C=C bond is restricted and each carbon carries two different groups. Partial hydrogenation of an alkyne on Lindlar's catalyst adds both H atoms from the same side (syn addition), giving the cis-alkene; reduction by sodium in liquid ammonia gives the trans-alkene.
Why: In cis-but-2-ene the two C–CH₃ bond dipoles do not cancel, so the molecule is slightly polar, giving stronger intermolecular forces and a higher boiling point (about 277 K against 274 K). The more symmetrical trans isomer fits better into the crystal lattice, so it has the higher melting point (about 167 K against 134 K).
Why not the others: (A) The poisoned catalyst and the Na/NH₃ method both stop at the alkene. (B) Reverses the two methods. (D) The isomers differ in polarity and shape, so their physical properties differ.
Key point: Lindlar gives cis, Na/NH₃ gives trans; cis has the higher boiling point, trans the higher melting point.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Products of adding HBr to propene with and without peroxide, and why HCl and HI show no peroxide effect
questions.question:
The table shows the major product when hydrogen halides are added to propene under different conditions.
| Reagent | Condition | Major product |
|---|---|---|
| HBr | no peroxide | 2-bromopropane |
| HBr | benzoyl peroxide present | 1-bromopropane |
| HCl | benzoyl peroxide present | 2-chloropropane |
| HI | benzoyl peroxide present | 2-iodopropane |
Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) Peroxide reverses the orientation of addition for all hydrogen halides

B) Without peroxide, HBr adds by an ionic mechanism through the more stable secondary carbocation (Markovnikov); with peroxide it adds by a free-radical mechanism through the more stable secondary radical, putting Br on the end carbon (anti-Markovnikov); for HCl and HI one step of the radical chain is unfavourable, so they still follow Markovnikov's rule
C) With peroxide, HBr adds through a primary carbocation
D) In every case the hydrogen goes to the carbon that has fewer hydrogen atoms
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Ionic addition (Markovnikov) without peroxide; radical addition (anti-Markovnikov) with peroxide, seen only for HBr.
Concept: Markovnikov's rule: the negative part of the reagent adds to the double-bond carbon with fewer hydrogens, because the reaction goes through the more stable carbocation. In the peroxide (Kharasch) effect, a bromine atom adds first, giving the more stable carbon radical, and the H is added afterwards.
Why: Ionic: H⁺ adds to CH₂, giving CH₃–C⁺H–CH₃; Br⁻ then attacks C-2. Radical: Br· adds to CH₂, giving the secondary radical CH₃–ĊH–CH₂Br, which takes H from HBr, so Br ends up on C-1. The H–Cl bond is too strong for H transfer to a radical, and an iodine atom adds to the alkene too slowly, so the chain fails for HCl and HI.
Why not the others: (A) The table shows that HCl and HI are unaffected. (C) The peroxide pathway involves radicals, not carbocations. (D) In 1-bromopropane the H has gone to C-2, which has fewer H atoms, so the rule as stated is contradicted.
Key point: Peroxide effect: HBr only; radical mechanism gives anti-Markovnikov product.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Observations in a zinc–silver galvanic cell: emf, electrode reactions, electron flow and the salt bridge
questions.question: A galvanic cell is set up as Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(1 M) || Ag⁺(1 M) | Ag(s) at 298 K, with a salt bridge of KNO₃. (E°: Zn²⁺/Zn = −0.76 V; Ag⁺/Ag = +0.80 V.) Which observation is correct?
options: A) The cell emf is 0.04 V, and silver dissolves while zinc is deposited
B) Electrons flow through the wire from the silver electrode to the zinc electrode

C) The emf is 1.56 V; zinc dissolves (anode) and silver is deposited on the silver electrode (cathode); electrons flow through the wire from zinc to silver; nitrate ions from the salt bridge move into the zinc half-cell
D) The emf is 2.36 V, because the silver half-reaction is doubled in the balanced equation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1.56 V; Zn dissolves, Ag deposits; electrons Zn → Ag; NO₃⁻ moves to the Zn side.
Concept: In a galvanic cell the electrode with the lower reduction potential is the anode (oxidation) and the other is the cathode (reduction). E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode. Electrode potentials are intensive, so they are not multiplied when the equation is multiplied.
Why: E°cell = 0.80 − (−0.76) = 1.56 V. Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ at the anode; 2Ag⁺ + 2e⁻ → 2Ag at the cathode. Electrons leave the zinc through the wire. As Zn²⁺ builds up and Ag⁺ is used up, anions from the salt bridge move into the zinc compartment and K⁺ into the silver compartment, keeping both solutions neutral.
Why not the others: (A) Subtracts the magnitudes and reverses the reaction. (B) Electrons flow from the anode (Zn) to the cathode (Ag). (D) E° values are not multiplied by stoichiometric coefficients.
Key point: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode; electrons flow anode → cathode in the wire; salt bridge anions move to the anode side.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Linear fall of concentration, half-life proportional to the initial concentration, and surface saturation in zero-order reactions
questions.question: Which statement about a zero-order reaction A → products is correct?
options: A) The rate does not depend on [A]; [A] falls linearly with time, [A] = [A]₀ − kt; the half-life [A]₀/2k is proportional to the initial concentration, and the reaction is complete at t = [A]₀/k; decomposition of ammonia on a hot platinum surface at high pressure behaves this way because the surface is saturated
B) The half-life is independent of the initial concentration
C) The graph of ln [A] against time is a straight line with slope −k
D) The rate constant has units of s⁻¹, as for every reaction
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Rate independent of [A]; linear fall; t½ = [A]₀/2k; complete at [A]₀/k; example: NH₃ on hot Pt.
Concept: For a zero-order reaction, rate = k[A]⁰ = k. Integrating −d[A]/dt = k gives [A] = [A]₀ − kt. The units of k are mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹.
Why: Setting [A] = [A]₀/2 gives t½ = [A]₀/2k, so doubling the starting concentration doubles the half-life. [A] reaches zero at t = [A]₀/k, after which the formula no longer applies. On a metal surface fully covered by adsorbed molecules, the rate is set by the fixed number of active sites, not by the gas pressure.
Why not the others: (B) A constant half-life is the mark of a first-order reaction. (C) A straight ln [A]–t graph is also first order; for zero order, [A] itself against t is a straight line. (D) Zero-order k has units of concentration per time.
Key point: Zero order: [A] = [A]₀ − kt; t½ = [A]₀/2k ∝ [A]₀; k in mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Counting coloured ions from their d-electron configurations, and finding the largest spin-only magnetic moment
questions.question: Consider the aqueous ions Sc³⁺, Ti³⁺, V³⁺, Cu⁺, Mn²⁺, Zn²⁺ and Cu²⁺. (Atomic numbers: Sc 21, Ti 22, V 23, Mn 25, Cu 29, Zn 30.) How many of them are coloured, and which has the largest spin-only magnetic moment?
options: A) 3 coloured; Cu²⁺ with 1.73 BM
B) 7 coloured; Zn²⁺ with 5.92 BM
C) 4 coloured; V³⁺ with 2.83 BM
D) 4 coloured; Mn²⁺ with 5.92 BM
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 4 coloured; Mn²⁺, 5.92 BM.
Concept: Transition metal ions are coloured when they have partly filled d orbitals, so that d–d transitions absorb visible light. Ions with d⁰ or d¹⁰ configurations are colourless. Spin-only moment μ = √[n(n + 2)] BM, where n is the number of unpaired electrons.
Given: Sc³⁺ 3d⁰; Ti³⁺ 3d¹; V³⁺ 3d²; Cu⁺ 3d¹⁰; Mn²⁺ 3d⁵; Zn²⁺ 3d¹⁰; Cu²⁺ 3d⁹.
Formula/Principle: coloured if 0 < number of d electrons < 10; μ = √[n(n + 2)].
Step 1: Coloured: Ti³⁺, V³⁺, Mn²⁺, Cu²⁺ = 4. Colourless: Sc³⁺, Cu⁺, Zn²⁺.
Step 2: Mn²⁺ (d⁵, high spin in water) has n = 5: μ = √35 ≈ 5.92 BM, the largest; V³⁺ has n = 2 (2.83 BM); Ti³⁺ and Cu²⁺ have n = 1 (1.73 BM).
Why: Half-filled d⁵ has the most unpaired electrons possible for a 3d ion. Mn²⁺ is coloured only faintly (pale pink), because its d–d transitions are spin-forbidden, but it is still counted as coloured.
Why not the others: (A) Misses V³⁺ and Mn²⁺ among the coloured ions, and Cu²⁺ has only one unpaired electron. (B) d⁰ and d¹⁰ ions are colourless, and Zn²⁺ has no unpaired electrons. (C) The count is right, but V³⁺ has fewer unpaired electrons than Mn²⁺.
Key point: d⁰ and d¹⁰ ions are colourless; μ = √[n(n + 2)], largest for d⁵.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Using measured magnetic moments of [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ and [FeF₆]³⁻ to decide between inner and outer orbital hybridisation
questions.question: Measurements on a Gouy balance show that K₃[Fe(CN)₆] has a magnetic moment of about 1.7–2.3 BM, while K₃[FeF₆] has about 5.9 BM. Both complex ions are octahedral. (Fe: Z = 26.) Which interpretation, using valence bond theory, is correct?
options: A) Both complexes use sp³d² hybrid orbitals and have five unpaired electrons

B) In [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ the strong-field CN⁻ ligands force the 3d electrons of Fe³⁺ to pair, leaving one unpaired electron and two empty 3d orbitals for d²sp³ (inner orbital, low spin) bonding; in [FeF₆]³⁻ the five 3d electrons stay unpaired and the complex uses sp³d² (outer orbital, high spin) hybrids
C) [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ is tetrahedral with sp³ hybridisation
D) [FeF₆]³⁻ is diamagnetic, because F⁻ is a strong-field ligand
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻: d²sp³, low spin, 1 unpaired; [FeF₆]³⁻: sp³d², high spin, 5 unpaired.
Concept: Fe³⁺ is 3d⁵. In valence bond theory, an octahedral complex uses either two inner 3d orbitals (d²sp³, inner orbital complex) or two outer 4d orbitals (sp³d², outer orbital complex). A magnetic moment of √[n(n + 2)] BM tells the number of unpaired electrons n.
Why: 1.73 BM corresponds to n = 1: the five 3d electrons are squeezed into three orbitals (2, 2, 1), freeing two 3d orbitals for d²sp³. 5.92 BM corresponds to n = 5: all 3d orbitals are singly occupied, so 4d orbitals are used (sp³d²). The measured value for the cyanide complex is a little above 1.73 BM because of orbital contribution, but it clearly indicates one unpaired electron. On the Gouy balance, the fluoride complex is pulled much more strongly into the field.
Why not the others: (A) The moment of the cyanide complex rules out five unpaired electrons. (C) Both complexes are stated to be octahedral, with six ligands. (D) F⁻ is a weak-field ligand, and 5.9 BM means five unpaired electrons.
Key point: Strong field (CN⁻): pairing, inner d²sp³, low spin; weak field (F⁻): outer sp³d², high spin.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Ordering ligands in the spectrochemical series from absorption wavelengths of cobalt(III) complexes, and finding the splitting energy
questions.question:
The table gives the wavelength of maximum absorption for four octahedral cobalt(III) complexes.
| Complex | λ(max) absorbed / nm |
|---|---|
| [CoF₆]³⁻ | 700 |
| [Co(H₂O)₆]³⁺ | 600 |
| [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ | 475 |
| [Co(CN)₆]³⁻ | 310 |
What is the order of crystal field splitting caused by the ligands, and what is Δo for [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ in kJ mol⁻¹? (N_A hc = 1.196 × 10⁵ kJ nm mol⁻¹)
options: A) F⁻ > H₂O > NH₃ > CN⁻; about 171 kJ mol⁻¹
B) CN⁻ > NH₃ > H₂O > F⁻; about 252 kJ mol⁻¹
C) CN⁻ > NH₃ > H₂O > F⁻; about 475 kJ mol⁻¹
D) NH₃ > CN⁻ > F⁻ > H₂O; about 252 kJ mol⁻¹
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) CN⁻ > NH₃ > H₂O > F⁻; Δo ≈ 252 kJ mol⁻¹.
Concept: In an octahedral field the d orbitals split into a lower t₂g set and an upper e_g set, separated by Δo. A d–d transition absorbs light of energy Δo, so a shorter absorbed wavelength means a larger splitting. Arranging ligands by the splitting they cause gives the spectrochemical series. The colour seen is complementary to the colour absorbed.
Given: λ = 700, 600, 475 and 310 nm; N_A hc = 1.196 × 10⁵ kJ nm mol⁻¹.
Formula/Principle: Δo = N_A hc/λ.
Step 1: Shorter λ means larger Δo: CN⁻ (310) > NH₃ (475) > H₂O (600) > F⁻ (700).
Step 2: Δo = 1.196 × 10⁵ ÷ 475 ≈ 252 kJ mol⁻¹.
Why: This order matches the spectrochemical series: halides are weak-field ligands, water intermediate, ammonia stronger and cyanide very strong.
Why not the others: (A) Reverses the order (treats longer λ as larger splitting) and uses 1.196 × 10⁵ ÷ 700. (C) The order is right, but the wavelength is used as if it were the energy. (D) Does not follow the trend in wavelength.
Key point: Δo = N_A hc/λ; shorter wavelength absorbed means stronger-field ligand.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Effect of nitro groups at ortho and para positions on the hydrolysis of chlorobenzene, and its directive influence
questions.question: Four compounds are heated with aqueous sodium hydroxide (or water) under the conditions shown, and the formation of the corresponding phenol is noted. Chlorobenzene: no reaction on boiling; reacts only at about 623 K and 300 atm. 4-Nitrochlorobenzene: reacts at about 443 K. 2,4-Dinitrochlorobenzene: reacts at about 368 K. 2,4,6-Trinitrochlorobenzene: reacts with warm water. Which conclusion is correct?
options: A) Nitro groups make the C–Cl bond stronger, so substitution becomes harder as more are added
B) Chlorobenzene reacts easily by an SN1 mechanism, like tert-butyl chloride
C) Nitro groups at the meta position are the most effective at activating the C–Cl bond

D) Nitro groups at ortho and para positions withdraw electron density and stabilise the negatively charged intermediate formed when OH⁻ attacks, so each additional o- or p-nitro group makes substitution easier; plain chlorobenzene is unreactive because the C–Cl bond has partial double-bond character from resonance; in electrophilic substitution, Cl is deactivating but ortho/para directing
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) o/p-nitro groups stabilise the anionic intermediate and speed up substitution; Cl deactivates the ring but directs o/p.
Concept: In haloarenes, the lone pair on Cl is delocalised into the ring, giving the C–Cl bond partial double-bond character and making nucleophilic substitution very difficult. Strong electron-withdrawing groups at ortho or para positions stabilise the negative charge (carbanion) formed when the nucleophile adds, by delocalising it onto the nitro group.
Why: The reaction conditions become milder as more o/p-nitro groups are added, from 623 K to warm water. A meta-nitro group cannot take part in this resonance. In electrophilic substitution, Cl withdraws electrons inductively (deactivating) but donates by resonance to the o/p positions (directing).
Why not the others: (A) The data show that each nitro group makes substitution easier. (B) The phenyl cation is very unstable, so SN1 does not occur for chlorobenzene. (C) The negative charge can be delocalised onto nitro groups only at the ortho and para positions.
Key point: o/p electron-withdrawing groups activate haloarenes towards nucleophilic substitution; Cl is o/p directing but deactivating.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Telling the isomeric butanols apart from their products when the vapour is passed over heated copper at 573 K
questions.question: Three alcohols P, Q and R, all C₄H₁₀O, are passed separately as vapour over copper heated to 573 K. P gives 2-methylpropanal, Q gives butan-2-one, and R gives 2-methylpropene. What are P, Q and R?
options: A) P is 2-methylpropan-1-ol (primary), Q is butan-2-ol (secondary), R is 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tertiary); hot copper dehydrogenates primary alcohols to aldehydes and secondary alcohols to ketones, but dehydrates tertiary alcohols to alkenes
B) P is butan-1-ol, Q is 2-methylpropan-1-ol, R is butan-2-ol
C) P is butan-2-ol, Q is 2-methylpropan-2-ol, R is butan-1-ol
D) All three are primary alcohols, since hot copper reacts only with primary alcohols
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) P: 2-methylpropan-1-ol; Q: butan-2-ol; R: 2-methylpropan-2-ol.
Concept: Heated copper at 573 K removes two hydrogens (one from O–H and one from the carbon bearing OH) from primary and secondary alcohols. A primary alcohol (–CH₂OH) gives an aldehyde; a secondary alcohol (>CHOH) gives a ketone. A tertiary alcohol has no H on the carbinol carbon, so it loses water instead and gives an alkene.
Why: 2-Methylpropanal, (CH₃)₂CHCHO, comes from (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH. Butan-2-one, CH₃COCH₂CH₃, comes from CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃. 2-Methylpropene, (CH₃)₂C=CH₂, comes from (CH₃)₃COH by dehydration. The carbon skeleton is unchanged, so the product shows which isomer each alcohol is.
Why not the others: (B) Butan-1-ol would give butanal, not 2-methylpropanal; 2-methylpropan-1-ol cannot give a ketone. (C) A tertiary alcohol cannot give a ketone. (D) Secondary alcohols react to give ketones, and tertiary ones are dehydrated.
Key point: Cu at 573 K: 1° gives aldehyde, 2° gives ketone, 3° gives alkene.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Number of β-hydroxy aldehydes formed in a crossed aldol of ethanal and propanal, and which carbonyl compounds cannot act as the enolate
questions.question:
The table lists four carbonyl compounds with the number of α-hydrogens in each.
| Compound | α-Hydrogens |
|---|---|
| Ethanal, CH₃CHO | 3 |
| Propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO | 2 |
| Methanal, HCHO | 0 |
| Benzaldehyde, C₆H₅CHO | 0 |
A mixture of ethanal and propanal is warmed with dilute NaOH. How many different β-hydroxy aldehydes (aldols) can form? What happens when a mixture of methanal and benzaldehyde is treated with concentrated NaOH?
options: A) 2 aldols; methanal and benzaldehyde also undergo aldol condensation
B) 1 aldol; methanal and benzaldehyde give no reaction at all

C) 4 aldols (two from self-condensation and two crossed); methanal and benzaldehyde cannot undergo aldol reactions because they have no α-hydrogen, and with concentrated alkali they undergo a crossed Cannizzaro reaction (methanal is oxidised to formate, benzaldehyde reduced to benzyl alcohol)
D) 4 aldols; methanal is reduced to methanol and benzaldehyde is oxidised to benzoate
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 4 aldols; methanal and benzaldehyde undergo a crossed Cannizzaro reaction.
Concept: In an aldol reaction, a base removes an α-hydrogen to form an enolate, which adds to the carbonyl group of another molecule, giving a β-hydroxy aldehyde. In a mixture of two aldehydes that both have α-hydrogens, each can act as the enolate and each as the carbonyl acceptor, so four products are possible. Aldehydes without α-hydrogens undergo the Cannizzaro reaction (disproportionation) with concentrated alkali.
Why: The four aldols are: CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CHO (ethanal + ethanal), CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH(CH₃)CHO (propanal + propanal), CH₃CH(OH)CH(CH₃)CHO (propanal enolate + ethanal), CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₂CHO (ethanal enolate + propanal). In the crossed Cannizzaro reaction, methanal, being the more reactive aldehyde, is oxidised to formate, and benzaldehyde is reduced to benzyl alcohol.
Why not the others: (A) Counts only the two self-condensations; compounds with no α-H cannot form an enolate. (B) Ignores the cross products, and methanal and benzaldehyde do react, by the Cannizzaro reaction. (D) The count is right, but the redox roles are reversed: methanal is oxidised.
Key point: Two enolisable aldehydes give 4 aldols; no α-H means Cannizzaro, and HCHO is the one oxidised.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting pKb values of ethylamines, ammonia and aniline in water in terms of inductive effect, solvation, steric hindrance and resonance
questions.question: The pKb values of some bases measured in water at 298 K are: (C₂H₅)₂NH 3.00; (C₂H₅)₃N 3.25; C₂H₅NH₂ 3.29; NH₃ 4.75; C₆H₅NH₂ 9.38. Which conclusion is correct?
options: A) The tertiary amine is the strongest base, because it has the most alkyl groups
B) Aniline is a stronger base than ammonia, because the benzene ring donates electrons
C) Basic strength in water depends only on the inductive effect of the alkyl groups

D) The order of basic strength in water is (C₂H₅)₂NH > (C₂H₅)₃N > C₂H₅NH₂ > NH₃ > C₆H₅NH₂; alkyl groups raise basicity by their +I effect, but in water the tertiary amine is held back by poorer solvation of its cation and steric crowding, while in aniline the lone pair is delocalised into the ring
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Diethylamine > triethylamine > ethylamine > ammonia > aniline.
Concept: A lower pKb means a stronger base. Basic strength of amines in water depends on the +I effect of alkyl groups (which increases electron density on N), the solvation of the protonated amine by hydrogen bonding with water, and steric hindrance. In aromatic amines, resonance of the lone pair with the ring lowers basicity.
Why: The secondary amine has the best balance of +I effect and solvation. The tertiary ammonium ion has only one N–H to hydrogen-bond with water, and crowding makes the lone pair less available, so it falls below the secondary amine in water, though in the gas phase it is the strongest. Aniline's lone pair is partly delocalised over the ring, so it is much weaker even than ammonia.
Why not the others: (A) The data show the secondary amine is the strongest in water. (B) Aniline has the highest pKb, so it is the weakest base. (C) If only the inductive effect mattered, triethylamine would be strongest; solvation and steric effects also matter.
Key point: In water: 2° > 3° > 1° > NH₃ (ethyl series) > aniline; solvation and resonance matter, not only +I.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Observations that the open-chain structure of glucose cannot explain, and what D and L mean in Fischer projections
questions.question: Which observations show that glucose exists mainly as a cyclic hemiacetal, and which statement about D/L configuration is correct?
options: A) Glucose does not give Schiff's test and does not form an addition product with NaHSO₃, although it has an aldehyde group in the open chain; its pentaacetate does not react with hydroxylamine; it exists as two forms, α and β, that interconvert in solution (mutarotation); "D" means the –OH on the lowest asymmetric carbon (C-5) is on the right in the Fischer projection, and it says nothing about the sign of optical rotation
B) Glucose reacts with hydroxylamine to form an oxime, which proves it has no aldehyde group
C) D-glucose must rotate plane-polarised light to the left, because D stands for dextrorotatory
D) Fructose is an aldohexose with the same open-chain structure as glucose
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) No Schiff's or NaHSO₃ reaction, unreactive pentaacetate, α and β forms and mutarotation show the cyclic form; D refers to the configuration at C-5.
Concept: In solution, glucose forms a six-membered ring (pyranose) when the C-5 –OH adds to the C-1 aldehyde, giving a hemiacetal with a new asymmetric centre at C-1 (the anomeric carbon). In the Fischer projection, a sugar is D if the –OH on its lowest (highest-numbered) asymmetric carbon is on the right, as in D-glyceraldehyde.
Why: With very little free aldehyde present, glucose fails Schiff's and bisulphite tests. In the pentaacetate the C-1 –OH is acetylated, so the ring cannot open and no oxime forms. The α (m.p. 419 K) and β (m.p. 423 K) anomers change into an equilibrium mixture in water. D-glucose is dextrorotatory, but D-fructose is laevorotatory, so D/L and (+)/(−) are unrelated.
Why not the others: (B) Free glucose does form an oxime with hydroxylamine, showing that it can react as an aldehyde; it is the pentaacetate that does not. (C) D/L refers to configuration, not to the direction of rotation. (D) Fructose is a ketohexose.
Key point: Glucose: cyclic hemiacetal with α/β anomers; D means –OH on the right at C-5, independent of rotation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Molarity of concentrated sulphuric acid from its mass percentage and density, and the volume needed for a dilute solution
questions.question: A bottle of concentrated sulphuric acid is labelled "98 % H₂SO₄ by mass; density 1.84 g mL⁻¹". What is its molarity, and what volume of it is needed to make 1.00 L of 0.50 M H₂SO₄? (H₂SO₄ = 98 g mol⁻¹)
options: A) 10.0 M; 50 mL, adding water to the acid
B) 18.4 M; about 27 mL, adding the acid slowly to water with stirring
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 18.4 M; about 27 mL, acid added slowly to water.
Concept: Molarity = moles of solute per litre of solution. From a mass percentage and density: M = (density in g L⁻¹ × mass fraction) ÷ molar mass. On dilution, the moles of solute are unchanged: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂.
Given: mass fraction 0.98; density 1.84 g mL⁻¹ = 1840 g L⁻¹; molar mass 98 g mol⁻¹; target 1.00 L of 0.50 M.
Formula/Principle: M = 1840 × 0.98 ÷ 98; V₁ = M₂V₂/M₁.
Step 1: Mass of H₂SO₄ per litre = 1840 × 0.98 = 1803 g; moles = 1803 ÷ 98 = 18.4, so the acid is 18.4 M.
Step 2: V₁ = (0.50 × 1.00) ÷ 18.4 = 0.0272 L ≈ 27 mL.
Why: Dilution of concentrated sulphuric acid releases a great deal of heat; adding acid to a large volume of water lets the water absorb the heat safely, whereas adding water to acid can make it boil and spatter.
Why not the others: (A) Uses a wrong molarity and the dangerous order of mixing. (C) Molarity right but halves the volume (treats 0.50 M as 0.25 M). (D) Forgets to convert millilitres to litres when finding the molarity.
Key point: M = (1000 × density × mass fraction) ÷ molar mass; M₁V₁ = M₂V₂; add acid to water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity; s and p block trends
questions.sub_topic: Why boron, nitrogen and beryllium differ from heavier members of their groups in maximum covalency, and diagonal relationship
questions.question: Which statement explaining the unusual behaviour of the first element of a group is correct?
options: A) Nitrogen forms NCl₅ easily, just as phosphorus forms PCl₅
B) Boron forms [BF₆]³⁻ just as aluminium forms [AlF₆]³⁻

C) The first element of each group (Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F) has only 2s and 2p valence orbitals and no d orbitals, so its maximum covalency is 4; for example, boron forms [BF₄]⁻ but not [BF₆]³⁻, while aluminium forms [AlF₆]³⁻, and nitrogen forms NCl₃ but not NCl₅; small size and high electronegativity also make it differ, and some first elements resemble the second element of the next group (Li with Mg, Be with Al)
D) The first element of a group behaves differently because it is the largest atom in the group
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) No d orbitals limits covalency to 4; small size and high electronegativity; diagonal relationships.
Concept: Elements of the second period have only four valence orbitals (one 2s and three 2p), so they can form at most four covalent bonds. Elements of the third period and beyond can use vacant d orbitals to expand their valence shell. The first member is also much smaller, more electronegative and has a higher ionisation enthalpy.
Why: Boron in [BF₄]⁻ uses all four orbitals; aluminium can accept six F⁻ ions using 3d orbitals. Nitrogen stops at three bonds plus a lone pair in NCl₃; phosphorus can form five bonds in PCl₅. Similar charge-to-size ratios explain the diagonal pairs Li–Mg and Be–Al (for example, Be(OH)₂ and Al(OH)₃ are both amphoteric).
Why not the others: (A) Nitrogen cannot expand its octet, so NCl₅ does not exist. (B) Boron has no d orbitals, so it cannot hold six fluorides. (D) The first element is the smallest in its group, not the largest.
Key point: Second-period elements: maximum covalency 4 (no d orbitals); small size; diagonal relationship.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Conditional probability for a point chosen uniformly in the unit square, found as a ratio of areas
questions.question: A point (x, y) is chosen uniformly at random from the unit square \(0\le x\le1,\ 0\le y\le1\). What is the probability that \(x+y<1\), given that \(x<\tfrac12\)?
options: A) \(\tfrac12\)
B) \(\tfrac38\)
C) \(\tfrac34\)
D) \(\tfrac14\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\tfrac34\).
Given: \(\text{uniform distribution on the unit square (area 1)};\ E=\{x+y<1\},\ F=\{x<\tfrac12\}\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(E\mid F)=\dfrac{P(E\cap F)}{P(F)}=\dfrac{\text{area}(E\cap F)}{\text{area}(F)}\)
Step 1: \(\text{area}(F)=\tfrac12\times1=\tfrac12\)
Step 2: \(\text{area}(E\cap F)=\displaystyle\int_0^{1/2}(1-x)\,dx=\tfrac12-\tfrac18=\tfrac38\ (\text{a trapezium with parallel sides 1 and }\tfrac12,\ \text{width }\tfrac12)\)
Worked derivation: \[P(E\mid F)=\frac{3/8}{1/2}=\frac34\]
Check: \[\text{trapezium area}=\tfrac12\left(1+\tfrac12\right)\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac38\ \checkmark;\quad P(E)=\tfrac12<\tfrac34\text{, sensible since small x makes }x+y<1\text{ likelier}\]
Why: \(\text{conditioning on F replaces the whole square by the strip }x<\tfrac12\text{ as the new sample space}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{is the unconditional }P(E)\); (B) \(\text{is }P(E\cap F)\text{, not divided by }P(F)\); (D) \(\text{is the complement }P(x+y\ge1\mid x<\tfrac12)=1-\tfrac34\).
Key point: \(\text{geometric probability: }P(E\mid F)=\text{area}(E\cap F)/\text{area}(F)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Values of k for which the equation cos⁻¹x = k sin⁻¹x has a real solution, using the ranges of the inverse functions
questions.question: For which real values of k does the equation \(\cos^{-1}x=k\sin^{-1}x\) have a real solution x?
options: A) \(k\ge0\text{ or }k\le-2\)
B) \(\text{all real }k\ne-1\)
D) \(k>0\text{ only}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(k\ge0\) or \(k\le-2\).
