Given: \(s=\sin^{-1}x\in\left[-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2\right],\quad \cos^{-1}x=\tfrac\pi2-s\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x=\tfrac\pi2\text{ for }|x|\le1\)
Step 1: \(\tfrac\pi2-s=ks\Rightarrow(k+1)s=\tfrac\pi2\Rightarrow s=\dfrac{\pi}{2(k+1)}\ (k\ne-1)\)
Step 2: \(\text{need }|s|\le\tfrac\pi2\iff|k+1|\ge1\iff k\ge0\text{ or }k\le-2\)
Worked derivation: \[k=0:\ s=\tfrac\pi2,\ x=1,\ \cos^{-1}1=0\ \checkmark;\qquad k=-2:\ s=-\tfrac\pi2,\ x=-1,\ \cos^{-1}(-1)=\pi=(-2)\left(-\tfrac\pi2\right)\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[k=-\tfrac32:\ s=\frac{\pi}{2(-1/2)}=-\pi\notin\left[-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2\right]\Rightarrow\text{no solution}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the graphs of }\cos^{-1}x\text{ (decreasing from }\pi\text{ to 0) and }k\sin^{-1}x\text{ meet only when the required value of }\sin^{-1}x\text{ lies in its range}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{ignores the range restriction on }\sin^{-1}x\); (C) \(\text{is essentially the excluded interval (only its end points work)}\); (D) \(\text{misses }k=0\text{ and all }k\le-2\).
Key point: \(\text{use }\cos^{-1}x=\tfrac\pi2-\sin^{-1}x\text{ and then the range }[-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2]\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Two non-zero 2 × 2 matrices whose product is zero in one order but not in the other
questions.question: Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) \(AB=BA\), since both matrices are upper triangular
B) \(A^2=A\) and \(AB=B\)
C) \(AB=BA=O\)
D) \(AB=O\) but \(BA=A\ne O\), and \(A^2=O\) although \(A\ne O\); so matrix multiplication is not commutative and a product can be zero with neither factor zero
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(AB=O,\ BA=A,\ A^2=O\).
Given: \(A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\ B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\)
Formula/Principle: \((PQ)_{ij}=\sum_k p_{ik}q_{kj}\ (\text{row of P times column of Q})\)
Step 1: \(AB=\begin{pmatrix}0\cdot1+1\cdot0&0\cdot0+1\cdot0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\)
Step 2: \(BA=\begin{pmatrix}1\cdot0+0&1\cdot1+0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}=A\)
Worked derivation: \[A^2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\]
Check: \[\det A=\det B=0\text{, as it must be: if }PQ=O\text{ with }P,Q\ne O\text{, neither can be invertible}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{unlike real numbers, matrices can be zero divisors, and the order of multiplication matters}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{being triangular does not make matrices commute}\); (B) \(A^2=O\text{, not }A\); (C) \(BA=A\ne O\).
Key point: \(AB\ne BA\text{ in general; }AB=O\text{ does not imply }A=O\text{ or }B=O\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: First and second derivatives of a curve given parametrically by x = t + 1/t, y = t − 1/t
questions.question: A curve is given by \(x=t+\dfrac1t,\ y=t-\dfrac1t\ (t>1)\). What are \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) and \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) at \(t=2\)?
options: C) \(\tfrac53\) and \(\tfrac{32}{27}\)
D) \(\tfrac53\) and \(-\tfrac89\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\tfrac53\) and \(-\tfrac{32}{27}\).
Given: \(\dfrac{dx}{dt}=1-\dfrac1{t^2}=\dfrac{t^2-1}{t^2},\quad \dfrac{dy}{dt}=1+\dfrac1{t^2}=\dfrac{t^2+1}{t^2}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt};\quad \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}{dx/dt}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{t^2+1}{t^2-1}=\dfrac{5}{3}\text{ at }t=2\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{t^2+1}{t^2-1}\right)=\dfrac{2t(t^2-1)-2t(t^2+1)}{(t^2-1)^2}=\dfrac{-4t}{(t^2-1)^2}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{-4t}{(t^2-1)^2}\cdot\frac{t^2}{t^2-1}=\frac{-4t^3}{(t^2-1)^3}=\frac{-32}{27}\text{ at }t=2\]
Check: \[x^2-y^2=4:\ y'=\frac xy=\frac{5/2}{3/2}=\frac53;\ y''=\frac{y-xy'}{y^2}=\frac{\frac32-\frac{25}6}{9/4}=-\frac{32}{27}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the second derivative must be taken with respect to x, so the t-derivative of }dy/dx\text{ is divided by }dx/dt\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{inverts }dy/dx\); (C) \(\text{sign error; the hyperbola branch is concave down here}\); (D) \(\text{forgets to divide by }dx/dt=\tfrac34\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{d}{dt}\Big(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\Big)\Big/\dfrac{dx}{dt}\), not \(\dfrac{d^2y/dt^2}{d^2x/dt^2}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Failure of the second-derivative test when f'' = 0, shown by x⁴, x³ and −x⁴
questions.question: For \(f(x)=x^4,\ g(x)=x^3\) and \(h(x)=-x^4\), the first and second derivatives are all zero at \(x=0\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) All three have a point of inflection at \(x=0\)
B) Since the second derivative is zero, none of them has a local extremum at \(x=0\)
C) All three have a local minimum at \(x=0\)

D) f has a local minimum, g has no extremum (the derivative does not change sign) and h has a local maximum at \(x=0\); so the second-derivative test gives no conclusion when \(f''=0\), and the first-derivative test (sign change of the derivative) must be used
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) f: minimum; g: no extremum; h: maximum.
Given: \(f'(x)=4x^3,\ g'(x)=3x^2,\ h'(x)=-4x^3;\ \text{all derivatives and second derivatives are 0 at }x=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{first-derivative test: }f'\text{ changes from − to + gives a minimum, + to − a maximum, no change gives no extremum}\)
Step 1: \(f'=4x^3:\ -\text{ for }x<0,\ +\text{ for }x>0\Rightarrow\text{local minimum}\)
Step 2: \(g'=3x^2\ge0\text{ on both sides}\Rightarrow\text{no extremum (inflection)};\quad h'=-4x^3:\ +\text{ then }-\Rightarrow\text{local maximum}\)
Worked derivation: \[f(x)=x^4\ge0=f(0),\qquad h(x)=-x^4\le0=h(0),\qquad g(x)=x^3\text{ takes both signs near 0}\]
Check: \[f'''(0)=0,\ f^{(4)}(0)=24>0\ (\text{min});\quad g'''(0)=6\ne0\ (\text{inflection})\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(f''(c)=0\text{ leaves the nature of a stationary point undecided; the sign of the derivative on either side decides it}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(x^4\text{ and }-x^4\text{ do not change concavity at 0}\); (B) \(\text{a zero second derivative does not rule out an extremum}\); (C) \(g\text{ has no extremum and h has a maximum}\).
Key point: \(f''(c)=0\Rightarrow\text{second-derivative test fails; use the sign change of }f'\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting the real roots of a function defined by an integral, using its derivative from the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
questions.question: Let \(F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x(t^2-3t+2)\,dt\). How many real solutions does \(F(x)=0\) have, and what are the local extrema of F?
options: A) Three solutions; local maximum at \(x=2\) and local minimum at \(x=1\)
B) Exactly one solution, \(x=0\); local maximum \(F(1)=\tfrac56\) and local minimum \(F(2)=\tfrac23\)
C) Two solutions; local maximum \(F(1)=\tfrac56\) and local minimum \(F(2)=0\)
D) No solution; F has no local extrema
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Only \(x=0\); local max \(\tfrac56\) at 1, local min \(\tfrac23\) at 2.
Given: \(F'(x)=x^2-3x+2=(x-1)(x-2)\ (\text{Fundamental Theorem of Calculus})\)
Formula/Principle: \(F'(x)=f(x)\text{ for }F(x)=\int_a^xf(t)\,dt;\ \text{use the signs of }F'\text{ and the extreme values to count roots}\)
Step 1: \(F'>0\text{ for }x<1,\ <0\text{ on }(1,2),\ >0\text{ for }x>2\Rightarrow\text{max at 1, min at 2}\)
Step 2: \(F(x)=\tfrac{x^3}3-\tfrac{3x^2}2+2x;\ F(1)=\tfrac13-\tfrac32+2=\tfrac56,\ F(2)=\tfrac83-6+4=\tfrac23\)
Worked derivation: \[F(x)=\frac x6\left(2x^2-9x+12\right),\quad \text{discriminant }81-96<0\Rightarrow\text{only root }x=0\]
Check: \[F\text{ increases from }-\infty\text{ through }F(0)=0\text{ to }\tfrac56,\text{ dips to }\tfrac23>0,\text{ then rises: one crossing}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the local minimum value is positive, so after crossing at }x=0\text{ the graph never returns to zero}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{reverses max and min and assumes a cubic always has three roots}\); (C) \(F(2)=\tfrac23\ne0\); (D) \(F(0)=0\text{ always, and }F'\text{ changes sign at 1 and 2}\).
Key point: \(F'(x)=f(x);\ \text{sign of }F'\text{ plus extreme values counts the roots}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Evaluating a definite integral by splitting it into an odd part, which vanishes, and an even part read as an area
questions.question: What is the value of \(\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2}\left(x^3\cos x+|x|\right)dx\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 4.
Given: \(x^3\cos x\text{ is odd};\ |x|\text{ is even}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a}g(x)\,dx=0\text{ if g is odd};\quad =2\int_0^ag(x)\,dx\text{ if g is even}\)
Step 1: \(\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2}x^3\cos x\,dx=0\ (\text{areas above and below the axis cancel})\)
Step 2: \(\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2}|x|\,dx=\text{area of two right triangles, each with legs 2 and 2}\)
Worked derivation: \[2\times\tfrac12\times2\times2=4\]
Check: \[2\int_0^2x\,dx=2\cdot\frac{x^2}2\Big|_0^2=4\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{an odd function's graph is symmetric about the origin, so the signed areas on }[-a,0]\text{ and }[0,a]\text{ cancel}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{treats the whole integrand as odd}\); (C) \(\text{doubles the area again}\); (D) \(\text{counts only one triangle}\).
Key point: \(\text{split into odd and even parts; odd part over }[-a,a]\text{ is 0}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Ratio in which the xy-plane divides the segment joining two points, and the point of division
questions.question: In what ratio does the xy-plane divide the line segment joining \(A(2,3,-4)\) and \(B(1,-2,3)\), and at which point?
options: A) 3 : 4 internally, at \(\left(\tfrac{11}7,\tfrac{6}7,0\right)\)
B) 4 : 3 externally, at \((-2,-17,0)\)
C) 4 : 3 internally, at \(\left(\tfrac{10}7,\tfrac17,0\right)\)
D) 1 : 1, at \(\left(\tfrac32,\tfrac12,0\right)\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 4 : 3 internally, at \(\left(\tfrac{10}7,\tfrac17,0\right)\).
Given: \(A(2,3,-4),\ B(1,-2,3);\ \text{xy-plane: }z=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{section formula: point dividing AB in ratio }k:1\text{ is }\left(\dfrac{kx_2+x_1}{k+1},\dfrac{ky_2+y_1}{k+1},\dfrac{kz_2+z_1}{k+1}\right)\)
Step 1: \(z=0:\ \dfrac{3k-4}{k+1}=0\Rightarrow k=\tfrac43>0\Rightarrow4:3\text{ internally}\)
Step 2: \(x=\dfrac{4(1)+3(2)}{7}=\dfrac{10}7,\quad y=\dfrac{4(-2)+3(3)}{7}=\dfrac17\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{point}=\left(\tfrac{10}7,\tfrac17,0\right)\]
Check: \[z\text{-coordinates }-4\text{ and }3\text{ have opposite signs, so A and B are on opposite sides of the plane; ratio }=|{-4}|:|3|=4:3\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a positive k means the dividing point lies between A and B}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{inverts the ratio}\); (B) \(\text{external division would need A and B on the same side of the plane}\); (D) \(\text{the midpoint has }z=-\tfrac12\ne0\).
Key point: \(\text{ratio from the z-coordinates: }|z_A|:|z_B|\text{ when they have opposite signs}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Direction cosines of a line, its angle with the z-axis, and a point on it at a given distance
questions.question: A line passes through \(P(1,2,3)\) and has direction ratios \(2,-1,2\). What are its direction cosines, and which point on it is at distance 6 from P in the direction of these ratios?
options: A) \(\left(\tfrac23,-\tfrac13,\tfrac23\right)\); the point \((5,0,7)\)
C) \(\left(\tfrac23,-\tfrac13,\tfrac23\right)\); the point \((13,-4,15)\)
D) \(\left(\tfrac25,-\tfrac15,\tfrac25\right)\); the point \((3,1,5)\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) DCs \(\left(\tfrac23,-\tfrac13,\tfrac23\right)\); point \((5,0,7)\).
Given: \(\text{direction ratios }(2,-1,2);\ P(1,2,3);\ \text{distance }6\)
Formula/Principle: \(l,m,n=\dfrac{(a,b,c)}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}};\ \text{point at distance r: }(x_1+lr,\ y_1+mr,\ z_1+nr)\)
Step 1: \(\sqrt{4+1+4}=3\Rightarrow(l,m,n)=\left(\tfrac23,-\tfrac13,\tfrac23\right)\)
Step 2: \((1+6\cdot\tfrac23,\ 2-6\cdot\tfrac13,\ 3+6\cdot\tfrac23)=(5,0,7)\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{x-1}{2/3}=\frac{y-2}{-1/3}=\frac{z-3}{2/3}=6\ \Rightarrow\ (5,0,7);\quad \text{angle with z-axis}=\cos^{-1}\tfrac23\]
Check: \[\sqrt{4^2+(-2)^2+4^2}=\sqrt{36}=6\ \checkmark;\quad l^2+m^2+n^2=\tfrac{4+1+4}9=1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{direction cosines are the components of a unit vector, so multiplying by r moves exactly r along the line}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{direction ratios are not direction cosines (their squares add to 9)}\); (C) \(\text{moves 6 times the direction ratios, a distance of 18}\); (D) \(\text{divides by }|a|+|b|+|c|=5\text{ instead of }\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}\text{, and moves only one step of the direction ratios}\).
Key point: \(\text{DCs}=\text{DRs}/\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2};\ \text{point at distance r}=P+r(l,m,n)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Minimum and maximum of a linear objective over an unbounded feasible region
questions.question: Consider the constraints \(x+y\ge4,\ x+3y\ge6,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\), and the objective \(Z=2x+3y\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) Z has maximum 12 and minimum 9
B) Z has minimum 12 and no maximum
C) Z has minimum 9 at \((3,1)\) and no maximum, because the feasible region is unbounded and Z increases without limit
D) Z has neither a minimum nor a maximum
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Minimum 9 at \((3,1)\); no maximum.
Given: \(\text{corner points of the unbounded region: }(0,4),\ (3,1),\ (6,0)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{for an unbounded region, a corner value is the minimum only if the open half-plane }Z<Z_{\min}\text{ has no point in common with the region}\)
Step 1: \(x+y=4\text{ and }x+3y=6\Rightarrow2y=2,\ y=1,\ x=3\)
Step 2: \(Z(0,4)=12,\ Z(3,1)=9,\ Z(6,0)=12\)
Worked derivation: \[2x+3y<9\text{ with }x+y\ge4,\ x+3y\ge6:\ 2x+3y=\tfrac32(x+y)+\tfrac12(x+3y)\ge6+3=9\Rightarrow\text{no such point}\]
Check: \[(x,y)=(100,0)\text{ is feasible with }Z=200;\ Z\text{ is unbounded above}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{geometrically, moving the line }2x+3y=c\text{ towards the origin, the last point of contact is the corner }(3,1)\text{; moving it outward it never leaves the region}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{12 is not a maximum; Z grows without limit}\); (B) \(9<12\text{ is attained at }(3,1)\); (D) \(\text{Z has positive coefficients and }x,y\ge0\text{, so it is bounded below and attains its minimum}\).
Key point: \(\text{unbounded region: check the half-plane }Z<Z_{\min}\text{ (or }Z>Z_{\max})\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the base of a logarithmic function from one point on its graph, and a point on the inverse exponential graph
questions.question: The graph of \(f(x)=\log_a x\ (a>0,\ a\ne1)\) passes through the point \(\left(8,\tfrac32\right)\). What is a, and what is the value of the inverse function \(f^{-1}\) at \(x=\tfrac12\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(a=4;\ f^{-1}(\tfrac12)=2\).
Given: \(\log_a8=\tfrac32\)
Formula/Principle: \(\log_ab=c\iff a^c=b;\ \text{the inverse of }\log_ax\text{ is }a^x\)
Step 1: \(a^{3/2}=8=2^3\Rightarrow a=2^{3\cdot\frac23}=4\)
Step 2: \(f^{-1}(x)=4^x\Rightarrow f^{-1}(\tfrac12)=4^{1/2}=2\)
Worked derivation: \[\log_4 2=\tfrac12\iff4^{1/2}=2\]
Check: \[\log_48=\frac{\log_28}{\log_24}=\frac32\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the graphs of }\log_ax\text{ and }a^x\text{ are reflections in }y=x\text{, so }(8,\tfrac32)\text{ on one means }(\tfrac32,8)\text{ on the other}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\log_28=3\ne\tfrac32\); (C) \(\text{treats the logarithm as division: }8\div\tfrac32\); (D) \(\text{evaluates f, not its inverse}\).
Key point: \(\log_ab=c\iff a^c=b;\ f^{-1}(x)=a^x\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Repeated composition of the Möbius function (x − 1)/(x + 1), which has period 4 under composition
questions.question: Let \(f(x)=\dfrac{x-1}{x+1}\) (with x outside the finite set where some composition is undefined). Write \(f^{[n]}\) for f composed with itself n times. What are \(f^{[2]}(x)\) and \(f^{[2027]}(x)\)?
options: B) \(f^{[2]}(x)=-\dfrac1x\text{ and }f^{[2027]}(x)=-\dfrac1x\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(f^{[2]}(x)=-\dfrac1x;\ f^{[2027]}(x)=\dfrac{1+x}{1-x}\).
Given: \(f(x)=\dfrac{x-1}{x+1}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{find the period of }f\text{ under composition, then reduce }2027\text{ modulo that period}\)
Step 1: \(f(f(x))=\dfrac{\frac{x-1}{x+1}-1}{\frac{x-1}{x+1}+1}=\dfrac{(x-1)-(x+1)}{(x-1)+(x+1)}=\dfrac{-2}{2x}=-\dfrac1x\)
Step 2: \(f^{[4]}(x)=f^{[2]}\!\left(-\tfrac1x\right)=-\dfrac{1}{-1/x}=x\Rightarrow\text{period }4\)
Worked derivation: \[2027=4\cdot506+3\Rightarrow f^{[2027]}=f^{[3]}=f\!\left(-\tfrac1x\right)=\frac{-\frac1x-1}{-\frac1x+1}=\frac{-1-x}{-1+x}=\frac{1+x}{1-x}\]
Check: \[f^{[3]}=f^{-1}:\ y=\frac{x-1}{x+1}\Rightarrow x=\frac{1+y}{1-y}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{because }f^{[4]}\text{ is the identity, }f^{[3]}\text{ must be the inverse of f}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(f\text{ is not self-inverse}\); (B) \(f^{[2027]}=f^{[3]}\text{, not }f^{[2]}\); (C) \(\text{sign error in }f^{[2]}\text{, and }\tfrac{x+1}{x-1}=1/f(x)\text{, not }f^{-1}(x)\).
Key point: \(\text{find when }f^{[n]}=\text{identity, then reduce the exponent modulo n}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding cos 2x and tan²x when the ratio cos 3x : cos x is given, using the triple-angle formula
questions.question: If \(\dfrac{\cos3x}{\cos x}=\dfrac13\) (with \(\cos x\ne0\)), what are the values of \(\cos2x\) and \(\tan^2x\)?
options: A) \(\cos2x=\tfrac13,\ \tan^2x=\tfrac12\)
B) \(\cos2x=\tfrac23,\ \tan^2x=5\)
C) \(\cos2x=\tfrac23,\ \tan^2x=\tfrac15\)
D) \(\cos2x=\tfrac56,\ \tan^2x=\tfrac1{11}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\cos2x=\tfrac23,\ \tan^2x=\tfrac15\).
Given: \(\cos3x=4\cos^3x-3\cos x\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{\cos3x}{\cos x}=4\cos^2x-3=2(1+\cos2x)-3=2\cos2x-1\)
Step 1: \(2\cos2x-1=\tfrac13\Rightarrow\cos2x=\tfrac23\)
Step 2: \(\tan^2x=\dfrac{1-\cos2x}{1+\cos2x}=\dfrac{1/3}{5/3}\)
Worked derivation: \[\tan^2x=\frac15\]
Check: \[\cos^2x=\frac{1+2/3}{2}=\frac56:\ 4\cdot\frac56-3=\frac13\ \checkmark;\quad \tan^2x=\frac{1/6}{5/6}=\frac15\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{dividing the triple-angle formula by }\cos x\text{ leaves an expression in }\cos^2x\text{, which converts directly to }\cos2x\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{sets }\cos2x\text{ equal to the given ratio}\); (B) \(\text{inverts the ratio: }\tfrac{1+\cos2x}{1-\cos2x}=5\text{ is }\cot^2x\); (D) \(\text{gives }\cos^2x=\tfrac56\text{ as if it were }\cos2x\).
Key point: \(\cos3x/\cos x=2\cos2x-1;\ \tan^2x=(1-\cos2x)/(1+\cos2x)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: The largest integer dividing 3^(2n) − 8n − 1 for every positive n, proved by induction
questions.question: Let \(a_n=3^{2n}-8n-1\) for positive integers n. What is the largest positive integer that divides \(a_n\) for every \(n\ge1\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 64.
Given: \(a_1=9-8-1=0,\ a_2=81-17=64,\ a_3=729-25=704=64\times11\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{the answer divides }\gcd(a_2,a_3,\dots);\ \text{then prove divisibility for all n by induction}\)
Step 1: \(\gcd(64,704)=64\Rightarrow\text{the answer is at most 64}\)
Step 2: \(\text{Base: }a_1=0\text{ is divisible by 64. Assume }64\mid a_k=9^k-8k-1\)
Worked derivation: \[a_{k+1}=9^{k+1}-8k-9=9(9^k-8k-1)+64k=9a_k+64k\Rightarrow64\mid a_{k+1}\]
Check: \[a_4=6561-33=6528=64\times102\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the inductive step rewrites }a_{k+1}\text{ in terms of }a_k\text{ plus a multiple of 64}\)
Why not the others: (A),(C) \(\text{divide every }a_n\text{ but are not the largest such integer}\); (D) \(a_2=64\text{ is not divisible by 704}\).
Key point: \(\text{test small n to find the candidate, then prove it by induction}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Condition on p for the complex roots of x² + px + 4 = 0 to have arguments between π/3 and 2π/3
questions.question: For real p, the equation \(x^2+px+4=0\) has non-real roots \(z\) and \(\bar z\), with z in the upper half-plane. For which values of p does \(\arg z\) lie strictly between \(\dfrac\pi3\) and \(\dfrac{2\pi}3\)?
options: C) \(-2\sqrt3<p<2\sqrt3\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(-2<p<2\).
Given: \(z\bar z=|z|^2=4\Rightarrow|z|=2;\quad z+\bar z=2\,\mathrm{Re}\,z=-p\)
Formula/Principle: \(z=2(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\Rightarrow4\cos\theta=-p\Rightarrow\cos\theta=-\dfrac p4\)
Step 1: \(\text{non-real roots need }p^2-16<0\iff-4<p<4\)
Step 2: \(\tfrac\pi3<\theta<\tfrac{2\pi}3\iff-\tfrac12<\cos\theta<\tfrac12\iff-\tfrac12<-\tfrac p4<\tfrac12\)
Worked derivation: \[-2<p<2\ (\text{which lies inside }-4<p<4)\]
Check: \[p=0:\ z=2i,\ \arg z=\tfrac\pi2\ \checkmark;\quad p=2:\ z=-1+i\sqrt3,\ \arg z=\tfrac{2\pi}3\ (\text{boundary, excluded})\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{since the product of the roots is fixed at 4, the roots lie on the circle }|z|=2\text{ and only their angle changes with p}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{is only the condition for non-real roots}\); (B) \(\text{misses the negative values of p}\); (C) \(\text{solves }|\cos\theta|<\tfrac{\sqrt3}2\text{, which is the condition for }\tfrac\pi6<\theta<\tfrac{5\pi}6\).
Key point: \(\text{roots of }x^2+px+q\ (q>0)\text{ non-real lie on }|z|=\sqrt q\text{, with }\cos\theta=-p/(2\sqrt q)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: A system of linear inequalities whose solution region shrinks to a single point
questions.question: What is the solution set of the system \(x+2y\le4,\ 2x+y\le4,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0,\ x+y\ge\tfrac83\)?
options: A) The single point \(\left(\tfrac43,\tfrac43\right)\)
B) A triangle with vertices \((2,0),\ (0,2),\ \left(\tfrac43,\tfrac43\right)\)
C) The empty set
D) The line segment from \((2,0)\) to \((0,2)\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The single point \(\left(\tfrac43,\tfrac43\right)\).
Given: \(\text{first four inequalities: quadrilateral with corners }(0,0),\ (2,0),\ \left(\tfrac43,\tfrac43\right),\ (0,2)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{a linear function attains its maximum over a polygon at a corner}\)
Step 1: \(x+2y=4,\ 2x+y=4\Rightarrow x=y=\tfrac43\)
Step 2: \(x+y\text{ at the corners: }0,\ 2,\ \tfrac83,\ 2\Rightarrow\max=\tfrac83\text{, only at }\left(\tfrac43,\tfrac43\right)\)
Worked derivation: \[3(x+y)=(x+2y)+(2x+y)\le8\Rightarrow x+y\le\tfrac83,\ \text{with equality only when both are equalities}\]
Check: \[\left(\tfrac43,\tfrac43\right):\ \tfrac43+\tfrac83=4\le4,\ \tfrac83+\tfrac43=4\le4,\ x+y=\tfrac83\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the line }x+y=\tfrac83\text{ just touches the quadrilateral at one corner, so the region degenerates to a point}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{the points }(2,0)\text{ and }(0,2)\text{ have }x+y=2<\tfrac83\); (C) \(\left(\tfrac43,\tfrac43\right)\text{ satisfies all five}\); (D) \(\text{that segment has }x+y=2\).
Key point: \(\text{an extra inequality can cut a region down to a corner point}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding n from the sum of cubes, then the sum of squares for the same n
questions.question: If \(1^3+2^3+\cdots+n^3=3025\), what is \(1^2+2^2+\cdots+n^2\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 385.
Given: \(\sum_{k=1}^nk^3=3025\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sum k^3=\left[\dfrac{n(n+1)}2\right]^2,\quad \sum k^2=\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}6\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{n(n+1)}2=\sqrt{3025}=55\Rightarrow n(n+1)=110\Rightarrow n=10\)
Step 2: \(\sum k^2=\dfrac{10\cdot11\cdot21}{6}\)
Worked derivation: \[\sum_{k=1}^{10}k^2=\frac{2310}{6}=385\]
Check: \[55^2=3025\ \checkmark;\quad 1+4+9+16+25+36+49+64+81+100=385\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the sum of the first n cubes is the square of the sum of the first n integers}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{is }\sum k^2\text{ for }n=9\); (C) \(\text{is }\sum k^2\text{ for }n=11\); (D) \(\text{is }\sum k\text{, not }\sum k^2\).
Key point: \(\sum k^3=(\sum k)^2\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Slopes of the lines through the origin that make an angle of 45° with the line y = 2x
questions.question: Which lines through the origin make an angle of 45° with the line \(y=2x\)?
options: A) \(y=3x\text{ and }y=-\tfrac13x\)
B) \(y=x\text{ and }y=-x\)
C) \(y=\tfrac13x\text{ only}\)
D) \(y=\tfrac13x\text{ and }y=-3x\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(y=\tfrac13x\) and \(y=-3x\).
Given: \(m_1=2;\ \theta=45^\circ\)
Formula/Principle: \(\tan\theta=\left|\dfrac{m-m_1}{1+mm_1}\right|\)
Step 1: \(\left|\dfrac{m-2}{1+2m}\right|=1\)
Step 2: \(m-2=1+2m\Rightarrow m=-3;\quad m-2=-(1+2m)\Rightarrow3m=1\Rightarrow m=\tfrac13\)
Worked derivation: \[m=\tfrac13:\ \frac{\frac13-2}{1+\frac23}=\frac{-5/3}{5/3}=-1;\quad m=-3:\ \frac{-5}{1-6}=1\]
Check: \[\tfrac13\times(-3)=-1\Rightarrow\text{the two lines are perpendicular, as the two bisector-type lines at }45^\circ\text{ must be}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the absolute value gives two lines, one on each side of }y=2x\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{these make }\tan^{-1}\tfrac17\text{ and }\tan^{-1}7\text{ with }y=2x\); (B) \(\text{these make }45^\circ\text{ with the x-axis, not with }y=2x\); (C) \(\text{misses the second line}\).
Key point: \(\tan\theta=|(m-m_1)/(1+mm_1)|\text{ gives two slopes}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Number of common tangents to two circles as the distance between their centres varies
questions.question: Consider the circles \(x^2+y^2=1\) and \((x-a)^2+y^2=4\) with \(a\ge0\). How many common tangents do they have when \(a=2\) and when \(a=\tfrac12\), and for which value of a do they have exactly three common tangents?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2 and 0; \(a=3\).
Given: \(r_1=1,\ r_2=2,\ \text{distance between centres }d=a\)
Formula/Principle: \(d>r_1+r_2:4;\ d=r_1+r_2:3;\ |r_1-r_2|<d<r_1+r_2:2;\ d=|r_1-r_2|:1;\ d<|r_1-r_2|:0\)
Step 1: \(a=2:\ 1<2<3\Rightarrow\text{the circles cut in two points: 2 common tangents}\)
Step 2: \(a=\tfrac12:\ \tfrac12<1\Rightarrow\text{the small circle lies inside the large one: 0 common tangents}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{three tangents}\iff\text{external contact}\iff d=r_1+r_2=3\Rightarrow a=3\]
Check: \[a=3:\ \text{the circles touch at }(1,0)\text{; the common tangent there is }x=1,\text{ plus two direct tangents}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{as the centres separate, the circles go from one inside the other (0), to internal contact (1), to cutting (2), to external contact (3), to separate (4)}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(a=1\text{ gives internal contact (one tangent)}\); (B) \(\text{one circle inside the other has no common tangent}\); (D) \(a=2\text{ gives cutting circles, not contact}\).
Key point: \(\text{compare d with }r_1+r_2\text{ and }|r_1-r_2|\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Equation of a circle with centre on the x-axis passing through two given points
questions.question: A circle has its centre on the x-axis and passes through \((1,2)\) and \((3,4)\). What is its equation?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(x^2+y^2-10x+5=0\).
Given: \(\text{centre }(h,0);\ \text{points }(1,2),\ (3,4)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{equal distances from the centre: }(1-h)^2+4=(3-h)^2+16\)
Step 1: \(1-2h+h^2+4=9-6h+h^2+16\Rightarrow4h=20\Rightarrow h=5\)
Step 2: \(r^2=(1-5)^2+2^2=20\)
Worked derivation: \[(x-5)^2+y^2=20\iff x^2+y^2-10x+5=0\]
Check: \[(3,4):\ 9+16-30+5=0\ \checkmark;\quad (1,2):\ 1+4-10+5=0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the centre lies on the perpendicular bisector of the chord joining the two points, here intersected with the x-axis}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{sign error in the constant: }25-20=5\); (C) \(\text{centre at }(-5,0)\text{, not equidistant from the points}\); (D) \(\text{passes through the origin; }(3,4)\text{ gives }25-15\ne0\).
Key point: \((x-h)^2+y^2=r^2;\ \text{equate distances to find h}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Phase, directions and amplitude ratio of the electric and magnetic fields in a plane electromagnetic wave
questions.question: A plane electromagnetic wave travels in vacuum along +z, with its electric field along x and amplitude \(E_0=30\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}\). Which description of the graphs of \(E_x\) and \(B_y\) against z at one instant is correct? (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
options: A) \(B_y\) is a quarter-wavelength behind \(E_x\), with amplitude \(9.0\times10^{9}\ \mathrm T\)
B) \(E_x\) and \(B_y\) are sine curves in phase (maxima and zeros at the same z), in perpendicular planes, with \(B_0=E_0/c=1.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm T\); \(\vec E\times\vec B\) points along +z
C) \(B\) is along z, parallel to the direction of travel, with amplitude \(1.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm T\)
D) \(E_x\) and \(B_y\) are in phase but \(B_0=E_0c\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) In phase, perpendicular, \(B_0=1.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm T\), propagating along \(\vec E\times\vec B\).
Given: \(E_0=30\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}},\ c=3.0\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\ \text{travel along }+z,\ \vec E\parallel\hat x\)
Formula/Principle: \(E_x=E_0\sin(kz-\omega t),\ B_y=B_0\sin(kz-\omega t);\ B_0=\dfrac{E_0}{c};\ \text{direction of travel}\parallel\vec E\times\vec B\)
Step 1: \(B_0=\dfrac{30}{3.0\times10^8}=1.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm T\)
Step 2: \(\hat x\times\hat y=\hat z\Rightarrow\vec B\text{ along }+y\text{ when }\vec E\text{ is along }+x\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{E}{B}=c\ \text{at every point and instant}\Rightarrow\text{zeros and peaks coincide (in phase)}\]
Check: \[\text{energy densities: }\tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2=\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}\iff E=cB\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{electromagnetic waves are transverse: both fields are perpendicular to the direction of travel and to each other, and oscillate together}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{the fields are in phase in a travelling wave, and }E_0c\text{ is far too large}\); (C) \(\text{B is transverse, not along the direction of travel}\); (D) \(\text{the ratio is }E_0/B_0=c\text{, so }B_0=E_0/c\).
Key point: \(\vec E\perp\vec B\perp\text{velocity},\ \text{in phase},\ B_0=E_0/c\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Apparent position of an air bubble inside a glass sphere, viewed through one spherical surface
questions.question: A solid glass sphere (refractive index 1.5) has radius 10 cm. A small air bubble inside it lies on a diameter, 4.0 cm from the surface nearer to the observer. Where does the bubble appear to be, and where would a bubble at the centre of the sphere appear?
options: A) 6.0 cm from the surface (real image); a bubble at the centre appears at the surface
B) 2.7 cm from the surface; a bubble at the centre appears 6.7 cm from the surface
C) 4.0 cm from the surface, because a curved surface does not shift images
D) About 3.1 cm inside the glass from the near surface (virtual image); a bubble at the centre appears to be at the centre
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) About 3.1 cm inside the surface; a bubble at the centre appears at the centre.
Given: \(n_1=1.5\ (\text{glass}),\ n_2=1.0\ (\text{air});\ u=-4.0\ \mathrm{cm};\ R=-10\ \mathrm{cm}\ (\text{centre on the incident side})\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{refraction at a spherical surface: }\dfrac{n_2}{v}-\dfrac{n_1}{u}=\dfrac{n_2-n_1}{R}\ (\text{distances from the vertex, positive along the light})\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac1v+\dfrac{1.5}{4.0}=\dfrac{-0.5}{-10}=0.05\Rightarrow\dfrac1v=0.05-0.375=-0.325\)
Step 2: \(v=-3.08\ \mathrm{cm}\ (\text{virtual, on the glass side})\)
Worked derivation: \[u=-10:\ \frac1v+\frac{1.5}{10}=0.05\Rightarrow\frac1v=-0.10\Rightarrow v=-10\ \mathrm{cm}\ (\text{the centre})\]
Check: \[\text{rays from the centre meet the surface along the normal and pass undeviated, so they still appear to come from the centre}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the bubble at 4.0 cm appears a little closer to the surface, as with a flat surface, but the curvature changes the amount}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{sign errors give a real image}\); (B) \(\text{uses the plane-surface rule }u/n\text{ and ignores the curvature}\); (C) \(\text{refraction at the surface does shift the apparent position}\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{n_2}{v}-\dfrac{n_1}{u}=\dfrac{n_2-n_1}{R};\ \text{an object at the centre appears at the centre}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Focal length of the same glass lens in air, in water and in a liquid of higher refractive index
questions.question: A thin equiconvex lens of glass (n = 1.5) has both radii of curvature 20 cm. What is its focal length in air and in water (n = 4/3), and how does it behave in a liquid of refractive index 1.6?
options: A) 20 cm; 20 cm; converging with focal length 20 cm
B) 40 cm; 80 cm; it becomes invisible
C) 20 cm; 80 cm; it behaves as a diverging lens of focal length about −160 cm
D) 20 cm; 15 cm; converging with focal length 10 cm
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 20 cm; 80 cm; diverging, f ≈ −160 cm.
Given: \(n_g=1.5;\ R_1=+20\ \mathrm{cm},\ R_2=-20\ \mathrm{cm}\Rightarrow\dfrac1{R_1}-\dfrac1{R_2}=\dfrac1{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{lens maker's formula: }\dfrac1f=\left(\dfrac{n_g}{n_m}-1\right)\left(\dfrac1{R_1}-\dfrac1{R_2}\right)\)
Step 1: \(\text{air: }\dfrac1f=0.5\times\dfrac1{10}\Rightarrow f=20\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Step 2: \(\text{water: }\dfrac1f=\left(\dfrac{1.5}{4/3}-1\right)\dfrac1{10}=0.125\times\dfrac1{10}\Rightarrow f=80\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{liquid }1.6:\ \frac1f=\left(\frac{1.5}{1.6}-1\right)\frac1{10}=-0.0625\times\frac1{10}\Rightarrow f=-160\ \mathrm{cm}\]
Check: \[n_m=n_g=1.5\Rightarrow\frac1f=0\ (\text{no bending; the lens becomes invisible})\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the bending depends on the relative refractive index; when the surroundings are optically denser, a convex lens diverges light}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{the focal length depends on the surrounding medium}\); (B) \(\text{uses only one surface in air, and only a liquid with }n=1.5\text{ would make it invisible}\); (D) \(\text{multiplies instead of dividing by the relative index}\).
Key point: \(1/f\propto(n_g/n_m-1);\ n_m>n_g\text{ makes a convex lens diverging}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Frequency, speed and wavelength of light entering glass, and the refraction law obtained from Huygens' construction
questions.question: Light of wavelength 600 nm in air enters glass of refractive index 1.5. Using Huygens' principle, which statement is correct? (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
options: A) The frequency stays \(5.0\times10^{14}\) Hz, the speed falls to \(2.0\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and the wavelength becomes 400 nm; the wavefront bends towards the normal because the secondary wavelets travel more slowly in glass, giving \(\sin i/\sin r=v_1/v_2=n\)
B) The frequency falls to \(3.3\times10^{14}\) Hz and the wavelength stays 600 nm
C) The speed rises to \(4.5\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and the wavelength becomes 900 nm
D) All three (frequency, speed and wavelength) fall by the factor 1.5
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) f unchanged at \(5.0\times10^{14}\) Hz; \(v=2.0\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\); \(\lambda=400\) nm.
Given: \(\lambda_0=600\ \mathrm{nm},\ n=1.5\)
Formula/Principle: \(f=\dfrac c{\lambda_0};\ v=\dfrac cn;\ \lambda=\dfrac{\lambda_0}n;\ \text{Huygens: in time }t\text{, wavelets travel }v_1t\text{ and }v_2t\)
Step 1: \(f=\dfrac{3.0\times10^8}{6.0\times10^{-7}}=5.0\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}\ (\text{set by the source; unchanged})\)
Step 2: \(v=\dfrac{3.0\times10^8}{1.5}=2.0\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}};\ \lambda=\dfrac{600}{1.5}=400\ \mathrm{nm}\)
Worked derivation: \[\sin i=\frac{v_1t}{AB},\ \sin r=\frac{v_2t}{AB}\Rightarrow\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\frac{v_1}{v_2}=n\]
Check: \[v=f\lambda=5.0\times10^{14}\times4.0\times10^{-7}=2.0\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the wavefront enters the glass gradually; the part already inside moves more slowly, so the front swings towards the normal; as }n\to1\text{ the bending disappears}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{frequency does not change at a boundary}\); (C) \(\text{light slows down in a denser medium}\); (D) \(\text{only the speed and wavelength change}\).
Key point: \(\text{at a boundary f is unchanged; }v\text{ and }\lambda\text{ divide by n}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Number of spectral lines, the visible Balmer lines, and the excitation energy when hydrogen atoms are raised to n = 4
questions.question: Hydrogen atoms in the ground state are excited to the n = 4 level and then return to the ground state by all possible transitions. How many different spectral lines can be emitted, which of them are Balmer lines and what are their wavelengths, and how much energy was needed for the excitation? (R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹; E₁ = −13.6 eV)
options: A) 6 lines; two Balmer lines, at about 486 nm and 656 nm; 12.75 eV
B) 6 lines; three Balmer lines; 13.6 eV
C) 3 lines; one Balmer line at 656 nm; 12.75 eV
D) 4 lines; two Balmer lines at about 486 nm and 656 nm; 0.85 eV
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 6 lines; Balmer lines at about 486 and 656 nm; 12.75 eV.
Given: \(n=4\to\text{lower levels};\ E_n=-\dfrac{13.6}{n^2}\ \mathrm{eV}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{number of lines}=\dfrac{n(n-1)}2;\ \dfrac1\lambda=R\left(\dfrac1{n_f^2}-\dfrac1{n_i^2}\right);\ \text{Balmer: }n_f=2\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{4\times3}2=6\text{ lines};\ \text{Balmer: }4\to2\text{ and }3\to2\)
Step 2: \(4\to2:\ \dfrac1\lambda=R\cdot\dfrac3{16}=2.06\times10^6\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}\Rightarrow\lambda\approx486\ \mathrm{nm};\quad3\to2:\ R\cdot\dfrac5{36}=1.52\times10^6\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}\Rightarrow\lambda\approx656\ \mathrm{nm}\)
Worked derivation: \[\Delta E=E_4-E_1=-0.85-(-13.6)=12.75\ \mathrm{eV}\]
Check: \[\text{lines: }4\to3,4\to2,4\to1,3\to2,3\to1,2\to1=6\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each pair of levels gives one line; only transitions ending on n = 2 fall in the visible Balmer series}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{only two of the transitions end on n = 2, and 13.6 eV would ionise the atom}\); (C) \(\text{counts only a direct cascade }4\to3\to2\to1\); (D) \(\text{counts lines wrongly, and 0.85 eV is the binding energy at n = 4}\).
Key point: \(n(n-1)/2\text{ lines; Balmer ends on n = 2; }E_n=-13.6/n^2\ \mathrm{eV}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Explaining energy release in both fission and fusion from the binding energy per nucleon curve
questions.question: Which statement about nuclear fission and fusion is correct?
options: A) Energy is released in fission because the products have a smaller binding energy per nucleon than the original nucleus
B) Fusion of light nuclei can happen at room temperature, because nuclear forces are long-range

C) The binding energy per nucleon is greatest (about 8.8 MeV) near A ≈ 56; splitting a heavy nucleus (A ≈ 235) into two medium nuclei, or joining two very light nuclei, both raise the binding energy per nucleon, so both release energy; fusion needs very high temperatures so that nuclei can overcome their electrostatic repulsion
D) Fission and fusion both destroy nucleons, converting them into energy
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Both fission and fusion move nuclei towards the peak of the binding energy curve near A ≈ 56; fusion needs very high temperature.
Given: \(\text{BE/A: about 7.6 MeV for }A\approx235,\ \text{about 8.5 MeV for }A\approx90\text{–}140,\ \text{peak about 8.8 MeV near }A\approx56\)
Formula/Principle: \(Q=(\text{total BE of products})-(\text{total BE of reactants})=\Delta m\,c^2;\ \text{energy is released when products are more tightly bound}\)
Step 1: \(\text{fission of }^{235}\mathrm U:\ \Delta(\text{BE}/A)\approx8.5-7.6=0.9\ \mathrm{MeV}\)
Step 2: \(Q\approx235\times0.9\approx200\ \mathrm{MeV}\text{ per fission}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{fusion }^2\mathrm H+{}^3\mathrm H\to{}^4\mathrm{He}+n:\ \text{BE/A rises from about 1–2.8 MeV to 7.1 MeV, releasing about 17.6 MeV}\]
Check: \[\text{nucleon number is conserved in both: }235+1=A_1+A_2+\text{neutrons};\ 2+3=4+1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the BE/A curve rises steeply for light nuclei and falls slowly for heavy ones, so both joining light nuclei and splitting heavy nuclei move towards the peak; nuclei must approach within about }10^{-15}\ \mathrm m\text{ to fuse, which needs temperatures of about }10^7\ \mathrm K\text{ to overcome Coulomb repulsion}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{fission products have a higher BE per nucleon, not lower}\); (B) \(\text{nuclear forces are short-range, and the Coulomb barrier prevents fusion at room temperature}\); (D) \(\text{nucleons are conserved; the energy comes from the decrease in mass}\).
Key point: \(\text{energy is released when products move towards the BE/A peak near }A\approx56\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Choosing the graph whose slope has the SI unit kg m² s⁻² K⁻¹
questions.question: Which of the following graphs has a slope whose SI unit, in base units, is kg m² s⁻² K⁻¹?
options: A) Potential difference (y) against current (x) for a resistor
B) The product PV (y) against temperature T (x) for a fixed amount of ideal gas
C) Displacement (y) against time (x) for a moving body
D) Force (y) against extension (x) for a spring
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) PV against T for a fixed amount of gas (slope = nR, in J K⁻¹).
Given: \(\text{target unit: }\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}\,K^{-1}}=\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{unit of slope}=\dfrac{\text{unit of y}}{\text{unit of x}};\ 1\ \mathrm J=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}\)
Step 1: \(PV:\ \mathrm{Pa\cdot m^3}=\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}\cdot m^3}=\mathrm{N\,m}=\mathrm J\Rightarrow\text{slope in }\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\ (=nR)\)
Step 2: \(V/I:\ \Omega=\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}\,A^{-2}};\ x/t:\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}};\ F/x:\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}=\mathrm{kg\,s^{-2}}\)
Worked derivation: \[\left[\frac{PV}{T}\right]=\frac{\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}}{\mathrm K}=\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}\,K^{-1}}\]
Check: \[PV=nRT\Rightarrow\text{slope}=nR,\ \text{and }R=8.314\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the kelvin is a base unit in SI, so only a slope involving temperature can contain }K^{-1}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{the ohm has no temperature unit and includes }A^{-2}\); (C) \(\text{velocity: }\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\); (D) \(\text{spring constant: }\mathrm{kg\,s^{-2}}\).
Key point: \(\text{slope unit}=\text{unit of y}\div\text{unit of x};\ \mathrm{J}=\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Angle between two vectors from conditions on their sum, difference, dot and cross products
questions.question: Find the angle between two non-zero vectors \(\vec A\) and \(\vec B\) in each case: (i) \(|\vec A+\vec B|=|\vec A-\vec B|\); (ii) \(\vec A\cdot\vec B=|\vec A\times\vec B|\); (iii) \(|\vec A|=|\vec B|=|\vec A+\vec B|\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 90°, 45°, 120°.
Given: \(|\vec A|=A,\ |\vec B|=B,\ \text{angle }\theta\)
Formula/Principle: \(|\vec A\pm\vec B|^2=A^2+B^2\pm2AB\cos\theta;\ \vec A\cdot\vec B=AB\cos\theta;\ |\vec A\times\vec B|=AB\sin\theta\)
Step 1: \((\text{i})\ A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta=A^2+B^2-2AB\cos\theta\Rightarrow\cos\theta=0\Rightarrow\theta=90^\circ\)
Step 2: \((\text{ii})\ \cos\theta=\sin\theta\Rightarrow\tan\theta=1\Rightarrow\theta=45^\circ\)
Worked derivation: \[(\text{iii})\ A^2=A^2+A^2+2A^2\cos\theta\Rightarrow\cos\theta=-\tfrac12\Rightarrow\theta=120^\circ\]
Check: \[\text{(iii): two equal vectors at }120^\circ\text{ and their sum form an equilateral triangle}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each condition fixes }\cos\theta\text{ or }\tan\theta\text{ independently of the magnitudes}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{(i) would give }|\vec A+\vec B|>|\vec A-\vec B|\text{ at }0^\circ\text{, and (iii) at }60^\circ\text{ gives }|\vec A+\vec B|=\sqrt3A\); (B) \(\text{at }90^\circ\text{ the dot product is zero but the cross product is not}\); (C) \(\text{(iii) at }60^\circ\text{ makes the sum }\sqrt3A\).
Key point: \(\text{square the magnitudes: }|\vec A\pm\vec B|^2=A^2+B^2\pm2AB\cos\theta\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Impulse and average force on a ball that rebounds from a hard floor compared with one that stops in sand
questions.question: A 0.20 kg ball is dropped from a height of 5.0 m. In case 1 it hits a hard floor and rebounds with the same speed, the contact lasting 0.010 s. In case 2 it falls into sand and stops in 0.10 s. What is the impulse given by the surface and the average force from it (ignoring the ball's weight during contact) in each case? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
options: A) Equal impulses of 2.0 N s; average forces 200 N and 20 N
B) 4.0 N s and 2.0 N s; average forces 40 N and 20 N
C) 2.0 N s and 4.0 N s; average forces 200 N and 40 N
D) 4.0 N s and 2.0 N s; average forces 400 N and 20 N
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 4.0 N s and 2.0 N s; 400 N and 20 N.
Given: \(m=0.20\ \mathrm{kg},\ h=5.0\ \mathrm m,\ \Delta t_1=0.010\ \mathrm s,\ \Delta t_2=0.10\ \mathrm s\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{impulse }J=\Delta p=F_{\text{av}}\Delta t;\ v=\sqrt{2gh}\)
Step 1: \(v=\sqrt{2\times10\times5.0}=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}};\ p=mv=2.0\ \mathrm{N\,s}\)
Step 2: \(\text{case 1: }\Delta p=m(10-(-10))=4.0\ \mathrm{N\,s};\ F=\dfrac{4.0}{0.010}=400\ \mathrm N\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{case 2: }\Delta p=m(0-(-10))=2.0\ \mathrm{N\,s};\ F=\frac{2.0}{0.10}=20\ \mathrm N\]
Check: \[\text{weight }=2.0\ \mathrm N\ll400\ \mathrm N\text{, so neglecting it in case 1 is reasonable}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{reversing the velocity doubles the change in momentum, and a short contact time makes the force large; sand lengthens the stopping time}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ignores the rebound, which doubles the impulse}\); (B) \(\text{divides case 1 by 0.10 s instead of 0.010 s}\); (C) \(\text{swaps the impulses}\).
Key point: \(J=\Delta p\ (\text{rebound doubles it});\ F_{\text{av}}=J/\Delta t\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Power needed to drive a car up an incline at constant speed against friction, separating conservative and non-conservative work
questions.question: A car of mass 1000 kg moves up a road rising 1 m for every 20 m along the road, at a constant speed of 20 m s⁻¹, against a constant resistive force of 500 N. What power must the engine deliver, and how much of the engine's work per kilometre of road is stored as gravitational potential energy? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 20 kW; 5.0 × 10⁵ J per km.
Given: \(m=1000\ \mathrm{kg},\ \sin\theta=\tfrac1{20},\ v=20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\ f=500\ \mathrm N,\ s=1000\ \mathrm m\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{constant speed: }F_{\text{engine}}=mg\sin\theta+f;\ P=Fv\)
Step 1: \(mg\sin\theta=1000\times10\times\tfrac1{20}=500\ \mathrm N\Rightarrow F=1000\ \mathrm N\)
Step 2: \(P=1000\times20=2.0\times10^4\ \mathrm W\)
Worked derivation: \[\Delta U=mg\,(s\sin\theta)=10^4\times50=5.0\times10^5\ \mathrm J;\quad W_{\text{friction}}=500\times1000=5.0\times10^5\ \mathrm J\ (\text{lost as heat})\]
Check: \[W_{\text{engine}}=Fs=10^6\ \mathrm J=\Delta U+W_{\text{friction}}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{gravity is conservative, so work against it is stored and recoverable on the way down; work against friction (non-conservative) is dissipated}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ignores either gravity or friction in the power, and counts all the work as stored}\); (C) \(\text{counts the friction work as stored energy}\); (D) \(\text{uses }mg\text{ instead of }mg\sin\theta\text{ in the power}\).
Key point: \(P=Fv;\ \text{work against gravity is stored, work against friction is dissipated}\)

questions.sub_topic: Support reactions on a uniform beam carrying a point load, from force and torque balance
questions.question: A uniform beam 4.0 m long and weighing 200 N rests horizontally on two supports at its ends, A (left) and B (right). A load of 600 N is placed 1.0 m from A. What are the upward forces at A and B?
options: A) 400 N at A and 400 N at B
B) 250 N at A and 550 N at B
C) 550 N at A and 250 N at B
D) 600 N at A and 200 N at B
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 550 N at A and 250 N at B.
Given: \(L=4.0\ \mathrm m,\ W=200\ \mathrm N\text{ at 2.0 m},\ F=600\ \mathrm N\text{ at 1.0 m from A}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{equilibrium: }\sum F=0\text{ and }\sum\tau=0\text{ about any point}\)
Step 1: \(\text{torques about B: }R_A\times4.0=200\times2.0+600\times3.0=2200\Rightarrow R_A=550\ \mathrm N\)
Step 2: \(R_A+R_B=800\Rightarrow R_B=250\ \mathrm N\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{about A: }R_B\times4.0=200\times2.0+600\times1.0=1000\Rightarrow R_B=250\ \mathrm N\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[550+250=800=200+600\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the support nearer the load carries more of it; taking torques about one support removes that support's unknown force}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{splits the load equally, ignoring where it is}\); (B) \(\text{swaps the two supports}\); (D) \(\text{gives all of the load to A and all of the beam's weight to B}\).
Key point: \(\text{take torques about one support, then use }\sum F=0\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Which elastic moduli liquids possess, the range of Poisson's ratio, and what shear modulus measures
questions.question: Which statement about elastic moduli is correct?
options: A) A liquid has a bulk modulus but no shear modulus, because it cannot resist a steady change of shape; the shear modulus relates shear stress to the change of shape at constant volume; Poisson's ratio (lateral strain ÷ longitudinal strain) cannot exceed 0.5 for an isotropic material, the value 0.5 corresponding to no change in volume
B) Liquids have a large shear modulus, which is why they are hard to compress
C) Poisson's ratio can have any positive value, such as 2 or 3
D) The bulk modulus of a gas is zero, since gases are easy to compress
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Liquids have a bulk modulus only; the shear modulus measures change of shape; Poisson's ratio ≤ 0.5.
Given: \(Y=\dfrac{\text{longitudinal stress}}{\text{longitudinal strain}},\ B=-\dfrac{\Delta P}{\Delta V/V},\ G=\dfrac{\text{shear stress}}{\text{shear strain}},\ \sigma=-\dfrac{\text{lateral strain}}{\text{longitudinal strain}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{for a rod of length }l\text{ and side }d\text{ stretched by strain }\varepsilon:\ \dfrac{\Delta V}{V}=\dfrac{\Delta l}{l}+2\dfrac{\Delta d}{d}=\varepsilon(1-2\sigma)\)
Step 1: \(\text{a fluid flows under any steady tangential stress}\Rightarrow G=0;\ \text{it resists compression}\Rightarrow B>0\ (\text{water: about }2.2\times10^9\ \mathrm{Pa})\)
Step 2: \(\text{stretching cannot reduce the volume of a stable isotropic solid}\Rightarrow1-2\sigma\ge0\)
Worked derivation: \[\sigma\le\tfrac12;\qquad \sigma=\tfrac12\Rightarrow\frac{\Delta V}{V}=0\ (\text{incompressible, nearly true for rubber})\]
Check: \[\text{metals: }\sigma\approx0.3\Rightarrow\frac{\Delta V}{V}=0.4\,\varepsilon>0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{shear changes shape at constant volume, which a fluid cannot resist permanently; compression changes volume, which every fluid resists}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{liquids have no shear modulus; their resistance to compression is the bulk modulus}\); (C) \(\sigma>0.5\text{ would make the volume fall on stretching}\); (D) \(\text{a gas has a finite bulk modulus (equal to P for isothermal changes)}\).
Key point: \(\text{fluids: only B }(G=0);\ \sigma\le0.5\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Source temperature of a Carnot engine from its efficiency, the rise needed for a higher efficiency, and the COP of the reversed cycle
questions.question: A Carnot engine with its sink at 300 K has an efficiency of 40 %. What is the temperature of the source? By how much must the source temperature be raised (sink unchanged) to make the efficiency 50 %? If the cycle is reversed between the original temperatures to work as a refrigerator, what is its coefficient of performance?
options: A) 750 K; raise by 50 K; COP 0.67
B) 500 K; raise by 50 K; COP 2.5
C) 500 K; raise by 100 K; COP 1.5
D) 420 K; raise by 180 K; COP 1.5
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 500 K; raise by 100 K; COP = 1.5.
Given: \(T_2=300\ \mathrm K,\ \eta=0.40\to0.50\)
Formula/Principle: \(\eta=1-\dfrac{T_2}{T_1};\ \text{Carnot refrigerator: COP}=\dfrac{T_2}{T_1-T_2}\)
Step 1: \(0.40=1-\dfrac{300}{T_1}\Rightarrow T_1=\dfrac{300}{0.60}=500\ \mathrm K\)
Step 2: \(0.50=1-\dfrac{300}{T_1'}\Rightarrow T_1'=600\ \mathrm K\Rightarrow\text{raise by }100\ \mathrm K\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{COP}=\frac{300}{500-300}=1.5\]
Check: \[\text{COP}=\frac{1-\eta}{\eta}=\frac{0.60}{0.40}=1.5\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the Carnot efficiency depends only on the two reservoir temperatures; a reversible engine run backwards is the best possible refrigerator between them}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses }T_1=T_2/0.40\text{, and the COP }\eta/(1-\eta)\text{ is inverted}\); (B) \(\text{the rise to 50\% needs }T_1'=600\ \mathrm K\text{, and 2.5 is }1/\eta\text{, the heat-pump COP}\); (D) \(\text{uses }T_1=T_2(1+\eta)\text{, which is not the Carnot relation}\).
Key point: \(\eta=1-T_2/T_1;\ \text{COP}_{\text{ref}}=T_2/(T_1-T_2)\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Comparing numbers of molecules, rms speeds, densities and kinetic energies of hydrogen and oxygen at the same pressure, volume and temperature
questions.question: Two identical vessels at the same temperature contain hydrogen (M = 2 g mol⁻¹) and oxygen (M = 32 g mol⁻¹) at the same pressure. Which comparison (hydrogen : oxygen) is correct?
options: A) Number of molecules 1 : 1; rms speed 4 : 1; density 1 : 16; average translational kinetic energy per molecule 1 : 1
B) Number of molecules 16 : 1; rms speed 16 : 1; density 1 : 1; kinetic energy per molecule 16 : 1
C) Number of molecules 1 : 1; rms speed 1 : 4; density 16 : 1; kinetic energy 1 : 16
D) Number of molecules 1 : 1; rms speed 16 : 1; density 1 : 16; kinetic energy per molecule 1 : 1
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1 : 1; 4 : 1; 1 : 16; 1 : 1.
Given: \(\text{same }P,\ V,\ T;\ M_{\mathrm H_2}=2,\ M_{\mathrm O_2}=32\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(PV=Nk_BT;\ v_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{3RT/M};\ \rho=PM/RT;\ \bar K=\tfrac32k_BT\)
Step 1: \(N=PV/k_BT\Rightarrow\text{equal numbers (Avogadro's law)}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{v_{\mathrm H_2}}{v_{\mathrm O_2}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{32}{2}}=4\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{\rho_{\mathrm H_2}}{\rho_{\mathrm O_2}}=\frac{2}{32}=\frac1{16};\qquad \bar K\text{ depends only on T}\Rightarrow1:1\]
Check: \[P=\tfrac13\rho v_{\text{rms}}^2:\ \tfrac13\cdot\tfrac1{16}\cdot16=\tfrac13\cdot1\cdot1\ \Rightarrow\text{equal pressures}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{lighter molecules move faster but carry less momentum each, so equal numbers at the same temperature exert the same pressure}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{equal P, V and T give equal numbers of molecules}\); (C) \(\text{inverts the speed and density ratios and makes KE depend on mass}\); (D) \(\text{rms speed goes as }1/\sqrt M\text{, not }1/M\).
Key point: \(\text{same }P,V,T:\ \text{equal N and equal }\bar K;\ v_{\text{rms}}\propto1/\sqrt M\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Finding g and the radius of the bob from the slope and intercept of a T² against string length graph
questions.question: In a simple pendulum experiment, a student measures the length l of the string from the support to the top of the bob (not to its centre) and plots T² (y-axis) against l (x-axis). The points lie on a straight line of slope 4.0 s² m⁻¹ that, when extended, cuts the l-axis at l = −1.0 cm. What are g and the radius of the bob? (π² ≈ 9.87)
options: A) 4.0 m s⁻²; 2.0 cm
C) 2.5 m s⁻²; 1.0 cm
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) g = 9.87 m s⁻²; bob radius 1.0 cm.
Given: \(\text{slope}=4.0\ \mathrm{s^2\,m^{-1}};\ \text{l-intercept}=-1.0\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Formula/Principle: \(T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}},\ L=l+r\Rightarrow T^2=\dfrac{4\pi^2}{g}(l+r)\)
Step 1: \(\text{slope}=\dfrac{4\pi^2}{g}\Rightarrow g=\dfrac{4\pi^2}{4.0}=\pi^2\approx9.87\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\)
Step 2: \(T^2=0\text{ when }l=-r\Rightarrow r=1.0\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Worked derivation: \[T^2=4.0\,(l+0.010)\ \Rightarrow\ \text{at }l=0.99\ \mathrm m:\ T^2=4.0\ \mathrm{s^2},\ T=2.0\ \mathrm s\]
Check: \[L=1.00\ \mathrm m,\ T=2\pi\sqrt{1.00/9.87}=2.0\ \mathrm s\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the slope gives g regardless of the length error; the systematic error in measuring l shifts the line sideways and shows up as the intercept}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{takes the slope itself as g and doubles the radius}\); (B) \(\text{halves the intercept as if it were the diameter}\); (C) \(\text{uses }g=\pi^2/\text{slope}\text{, forgetting the factor 4}\).
Key point: \(T^2=(4\pi^2/g)(l+r):\ g\text{ from the slope, r from the l-intercept}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Torque and work for a dipole rotated in a uniform field, and how its field on the axis and equator scales with distance
questions.question: An electric dipole of moment p is placed in a uniform field E. Which statement is correct?
options: A) The work needed to turn the dipole from alignment with E to the opposite direction is pE, and the field of the dipole falls as 1/r²

B) The torque is greatest (pE) when the dipole is perpendicular to E; the work to turn it from parallel to antiparallel is 2pE; far from the dipole its field on the axis is twice that on the equatorial line at the same distance, and both fall to one-eighth when the distance is doubled
C) The torque is greatest when the dipole is parallel to E
D) The field on the equatorial line is in the same direction as p
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) τ_max = pE at 90°; work 2pE; axial field = 2 × equatorial; both ∝ 1/r³.
Given: \(\text{dipole moment }p\text{ in uniform field }E;\ r\gg\text{dipole length}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\tau=pE\sin\theta;\ U=-pE\cos\theta;\ E_{\text{axial}}=\dfrac{2kp}{r^3},\ E_{\text{eq}}=\dfrac{kp}{r^3}\ (\text{opposite to }\vec p)\)
Step 1: \(\tau_{\max}=pE\text{ at }\theta=90^\circ;\ \tau=0\text{ at }0^\circ\text{ and }180^\circ\)
Step 2: \(W=U(180^\circ)-U(0^\circ)=pE-(-pE)=2pE\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{E_{\text{axial}}}{E_{\text{eq}}}=2;\qquad r\to2r:\ E\to\frac{E}{8}\]
Check: \[W=\int_0^\pi pE\sin\theta\,d\theta=pE\left[-\cos\theta\right]_0^\pi=2pE\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the fields of the two opposite charges nearly cancel far away, leaving a field that falls faster than that of a single charge}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{work is 2pE, and the dipole field falls as }1/r^3\); (C) \(\text{at }\theta=0\text{ the torque is zero (stable equilibrium)}\); (D) \(\text{on the equatorial line the field is opposite to }\vec p\).
Key point: \(\tau=pE\sin\theta;\ W_{0\to180^\circ}=2pE;\ E_{\text{dipole}}\propto1/r^3,\ \text{axial}=2\times\text{equatorial}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Charges induced on the inner and outer surfaces of a hollow conductor, and electrostatic shielding
questions.question: A hollow metal sphere carrying a charge +Q stands on an insulating stand. A small charge +q, hanging from an insulating thread, is lowered into its cavity without touching the walls. Which observation is correct?
options: A) The charge +q is pushed out of the cavity, because the field inside a charged conductor is very strong
B) The inner surface acquires a charge +q and the outer surface keeps +Q
C) All the charges spread uniformly through the metal

D) Before +q is inserted, the field inside the empty cavity is zero and all of +Q is on the outer surface; with +q inside, a charge −q appears on the inner surface and the outer surface carries +Q + q, while the field in the metal itself stays zero
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Empty cavity: E = 0 and all charge on the outer surface; with +q inside: −q on the inner surface, Q + q on the outer surface.
Given: \(\text{conductor with net charge }+Q;\ \text{point charge }+q\text{ placed in the cavity without contact}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{electrostatic equilibrium: }E=0\text{ inside the metal; Gauss's law }\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A=\dfrac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0}\)
Step 1: \(\text{Gaussian surface inside the metal enclosing the cavity: }E=0\Rightarrow q_{\text{enc}}=0\Rightarrow q_{\text{inner}}+q=0\)
Step 2: \(q_{\text{inner}}=-q;\ \text{charge conservation: }q_{\text{inner}}+q_{\text{outer}}=Q\)
Worked derivation: \[q_{\text{outer}}=Q-(-q)=Q+q\]
Check: \[\text{empty cavity }(q=0):\ q_{\text{inner}}=0,\ q_{\text{outer}}=Q,\ \text{field in cavity}=0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{free electrons in the metal move until the field inside it vanishes; this is why a metal enclosure shields instruments from outside fields (electrostatic shielding)}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{there is no field inside the empty cavity to push the charge}\); (B) \(\text{the inner charge must cancel }+q\text{, so it is }-q\); (C) \(\text{in equilibrium, charge lies only on the surfaces}\).
Key point: \(\text{inner surface}=-(\text{charge in cavity});\ \text{outer surface carries the rest}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Drift speed of electrons in a copper wire and how it changes when the wire is made longer at the same applied voltage
questions.question: A copper wire of cross-sectional area 1.0 mm² carries a current of 1.6 A. Copper has 8.0 × 10²⁸ free electrons per m³. What is the drift speed? If the same voltage is applied to a wire of the same material and area but twice as long (same temperature), what happens to the drift speed? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
options: A) 1.25 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹; unchanged
B) 1.25 × 10⁻² m s⁻¹; halves
C) 1.25 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹; halves, because the field E = V/l halves
D) 0.125 m s⁻¹; doubles
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1.25 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹; it halves.
Given: \(A=1.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^2},\ I=1.6\ \mathrm A,\ n=8.0\times10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}},\ e=1.6\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm C\)
Formula/Principle: \(I=neAv_d;\ v_d=\mu E=\mu\dfrac Vl\)
Step 1: \(v_d=\dfrac{1.6}{8.0\times10^{28}\times1.6\times10^{-19}\times1.0\times10^{-6}}=\dfrac{1.6}{1.28\times10^4}\)
Step 2: \(v_d=1.25\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\ (\text{about 0.1 mm s}^{-1})\)
Worked derivation: \[l\to2l\text{ at the same }V:\ E=\frac Vl\to\frac E2\Rightarrow v_d\to\frac{v_d}{2}\]
Check: \[R\to2R\Rightarrow I\to\frac I2;\ v_d=\frac{I}{neA}\to\frac{v_d}2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{drift speed is set by the field inside the conductor (through the mobility), not by the voltage alone; the slow drift does not delay the current, because the field is set up almost instantly along the wire}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{the field, and so }v_d\text{, depends on the length at fixed voltage}\); (B) \(\text{the halving is right, but the value is 100 times too large (an error in converting the area)}\); (D) \(\text{a longer wire has a weaker field and smaller current}\).
Key point: \(v_d=I/(neA)=\mu V/l\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Comparing the magnetic fields inside two solenoids with the same turns and current but different lengths, from Ampère's law
questions.question: Solenoid P has 500 turns wound uniformly over a length of 0.25 m; solenoid Q has 500 turns over 0.50 m. Each is long compared with its diameter and carries 2.0 A. What is the field inside each, near the middle? (µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹)
options: A) 5.0 mT in P and 2.5 mT in Q; uniform inside and nearly zero outside
B) 2.5 mT in P and 5.0 mT in Q
C) 5.0 mT in both, since the number of turns and current are the same
D) 1.3 mT in P and 0.63 mT in Q
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 5.0 mT in P, 2.5 mT in Q.
Given: \(N=500;\ l_P=0.25\ \mathrm m,\ l_Q=0.50\ \mathrm m;\ I=2.0\ \mathrm A\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{Ampère's law on a rectangular loop with one side inside: }Bl=\mu_0(nl)I\Rightarrow B=\mu_0nI,\ n=N/l\)
Step 1: \(n_P=2000\ \mathrm{m^{-1}},\ n_Q=1000\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}\)
Step 2: \(B_P=4\pi\times10^{-7}\times2000\times2.0=5.03\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm T\)
Worked derivation: \[B_Q=\frac{B_P}2=2.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm T\]
Check: \[\text{units: }\mathrm{T\,m\,A^{-1}}\times\mathrm{m^{-1}}\times\mathrm A=\mathrm T\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the field depends on the turns per unit length, not on the total number of turns; the same turns spread over twice the length give half the field}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{reverses the dependence on length}\); (C) \(\text{uses N instead of }n=N/l\); (D) \(\text{uses }\mu_0nI/4\text{, the formula wrongly divided}\).
Key point: \(B=\mu_0nI\text{ with }n=N/l;\ \text{uniform inside, about zero outside}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Magnetic intensity, magnetisation and field inside a solenoid with an iron core of known relative permeability
questions.question: A long solenoid with 1000 turns per metre carries a current of 2.0 A. Its core is filled with iron of relative permeability 1000. What are the magnetic intensity H, the magnetisation M of the iron and the field B inside? (µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) H = 2.0 × 10³ A m⁻¹; M ≈ 2.0 × 10⁶ A m⁻¹; B ≈ 2.5 T.
Given: \(n=1000\ \mathrm{m^{-1}},\ I=2.0\ \mathrm A,\ \mu_r=1000\)
Formula/Principle: \(H=nI;\ M=\chi H=(\mu_r-1)H;\ B=\mu_0(H+M)=\mu_0\mu_rH\)
Step 1: \(H=1000\times2.0=2.0\times10^3\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\ (\text{set by the free current only})\)
Step 2: \(M=999\times2.0\times10^3\approx2.0\times10^6\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\)
Worked derivation: \[B=4\pi\times10^{-7}\times1000\times2.0\times10^3=2.51\ \mathrm T\]
Check: \[\text{air core: }B_0=\mu_0H=2.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm T;\ \text{iron multiplies it by }\mu_r=1000\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the coil current fixes H; the iron's atomic dipoles line up and add a magnetisation about a thousand times larger, greatly increasing B}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{swaps H and M and gives the air-core field}\); (C) \(\text{ignores the magnetisation of the iron}\); (D) \(\text{multiplies by }\mu_r\text{ twice}\).
Key point: \(H=nI;\ M=(\mu_r-1)H;\ B=\mu_0\mu_rH\)
